nuance.analogy: Daunt is like a steep hill seen from the bottom: it does not push you back, but the sight of it makes you hesitate.
nuance.etymology: From Old French danter, from Latin domitare, to tame.
common_mistakes: Using daunt as a noun, as in 'a daunt', instead of the verb.
Confusing daunt with don't, since both sound similar in casual speech.

daunt.etymology: From Middle English *daunten*, from Old French *danter*, *donter* (“to tame”), from Latin *domitō* (“tame”), frequentative of Latin *domō* (“tame, conquer”), from Proto-Italic **domaō*, from Proto-Indo-European **demh₂-* (“to domesticate, tame”).

senses.definition: All the time; round the clock; unceasingly.
Synonym of chalk and cheese (“two things that are very different”).

core.definition: Constantly, all the time, without stopping, including through the night.

pronunciation.tip: Stress NIGHT more than day, and reduce and to a quick uhnd. Link the words smoothly so the phrase sounds like 'day-und-NIGHT'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative when complaining, and positive when praising hard work or devotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'work day and night' or 'rain day and night' to mean constantly. The noun sense 'chalk and cheese' is mainly British; Americans say 'like night and day' to describe two things that are very different. A natural reply is 'Wow, you must be exhausted' or 'It's been non-stop around here.'

distinctions.note: Around the clock means 24 hours a day, often for operations or services; day and night emphasizes constant effort or an ongoing condition.
Constantly is a general word; day and night is more vivid and often suggests tireless effort.
Like night and day describes a contrast between two things, not continuous action.

collocations: think about it day and night

examples.everyday: My neighbor's dog barks day and night, and it's driving me crazy.
examples.professional: Our on-call team has been fixing the outage day and night since Monday.
examples.analytical: Monastic communities structured their prayer so that praise continued day and night, reflecting a theology of unceasing devotion.

nuance.analogy: Day and night is like a lighthouse that never switches off, keeping its beam going through every hour.
nuance.etymology: Both nouns come from Old English: dæg (day) and niht (night).
common_mistakes: Saying 'in day and night' instead of 'day and night'.
Using the phrase only for contrast, when it actually means constant action.
Using 'day and nights' with a plural, which is incorrect in this fixed expression.
nuance.biblical_note: Psalm 1:2 describes the righteous person as one who meditates on God's law day and night, using the Hebrew phrase yomam welaylah, 'day and night'. The idea shows a continuous, devoted attention to Scripture, and the phrase is familiar to many American churchgoers.

senses.definition: The position or role of a dean.

core.definition: The position, term or role of serving as a dean at a college or university.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DEEN. The -ship ending is short, with an unstressed vowel like the i in 'ship'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and institutional. It names a role rather than a person.
nuance.usage_note: Deanship appears mainly in academic and institutional writing, such as a university announcement that someone will assume the deanship next July. In casual conversation Americans say she's the dean or during his time as dean. The word refers to the role itself, not the person.

distinctions.note: A chairmanship leads one department or committee, while a deanship leads a whole college or school.
A presidency is the top office of a university, while a deanship is a division-level post below the provost and president.

examples.everyday: Since she took the deanship, she has hardly had time for lunch with her friends.
examples.professional: The search committee will announce its recommendation for the deanship by the end of the month.
examples.analytical: Her deanship was defined by an effort to decentralize budget authority, which reshaped relations between faculty and administration.

nuance.analogy: Like a captaincy on a ship: the title matters less than the responsibility for steering the whole crew.
nuance.etymology: From dean plus -ship, a suffix meaning office or position.
common_mistakes: Using deanship in casual talk to mean the person; say the dean or she is dean.
Confusing deanship with dean's office; the office is the physical location and staff, while deanship is the role.

senses.definition: A young woman who makes her first formal appearance in society.
A female debutant, especially in sport and entertainment.
senses.example: The rising debutante signed a contract with a major label after her first hit single.

core.definition: A young woman, traditionally from a wealthy family, formally introduced to society at a debut party or ball.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on DEB, with a weaker secondary stress on the last syllable. The middle syllable is 'yoo', and the final t is clearly pronounced, not 'tant' with a nasal ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, sometimes slightly dated, and can suggest privilege or old-fashioned social ritual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use debutante for the Southern and high-society custom of a debut ball, and the word appears in local news about cotillions and society events. Most Americans would not use it for a young woman starting her first job or public role. Traditionally it refers only to women; the male equivalent is rarely used.

distinctions.note: Debut is the first public appearance itself and can apply to anyone; debutante names the young woman being presented at such an event.
A socialite is known for attending parties at any age; a debutante is a young woman at her first formal society appearance.

examples.everyday: My cousin from Charleston is a debutante this year, so the whole family is going to the ball.
examples.professional: The magazine profiled the former debutante who now runs a nonprofit funding literacy programs.
examples.analytical: The debutante ritual signals a family's social standing, turning a young woman's introduction into a public display of inherited class.

nuance.analogy: A debutante ball is like a formal introduction card for a family's social name, presenting a young woman to the community.
nuance.etymology: From French débutante, the feminine of débutant 'beginner', from débuter 'to begin'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable (deb-yoo-TANT); the main stress is on the first syllable.
Using debutante for any young woman starting a career; the word refers specifically to a formal society debut.

senses.definition: In a decorous manner.

core.definition: In a polite, proper, and dignified way that matches the situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllables are weak, so the word sounds like 'DEK-uh-ruhs-lee' with the final -ly as a clear 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests dignity and restraint, but it can sound stiff in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'decorously' mainly in writing or formal description, such as 'The guests left decorously.' In everyday speech, 'politely' or 'properly' sounds more natural. It is rarely used with a casual tone.

distinctions.note: 'Politely' is everyday and warm; 'decorously' emphasizes dignity and suitability for a formal occasion.

examples.everyday: When the neighbors came over, the kids sat down and behaved themselves quite decorously.
examples.professional: Please address the committee decorously, even if you strongly disagree with the proposal.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the characters speak decorously because their society values restraint more than honesty.

nuance.analogy: Acting decorously is like walking carefully through a museum: you move with respect for the space and the people around you.
nuance.etymology: From decorous, from Latin decorus, 'proper, seemly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'decorously' in casual speech where 'politely' fits better.
Confusing it with 'decoratively', which refers to appearance.

senses.definition: Appropriate social behavior.
A convention of social behavior.

core.definition: Behavior that is socially correct and suitable for a formal or serious situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'KOR'. The first syllable is a weak 'dih', and the final syllable is a reduced 'uhm', not 'um' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it implies respect and self-control, but can sound stiff if used lightly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'decorum' in formal settings such as courts, legislatures, religious services, or meetings. They often say 'maintain decorum' or 'lose decorum'. In everyday speech, 'manners' or 'behaving yourself' is more common, and 'decorum' may sound overly formal.

distinctions.note: 'Manners' refers to everyday polite behavior, while 'decorum' focuses on behavior suited to a formal occasion.
'Etiquette' is a set of written or customary rules; 'decorum' is the general sense of proper conduct.

examples.everyday: The kids were being silly at the wedding, so their mom reminded them to keep some decorum.
examples.professional: The chair asked everyone to maintain decorum during the budget hearing.
examples.analytical: Decorum is not merely a set of rules but a shared understanding of how people owe one another respect in public life.

nuance.analogy: Decorum is like a stage's curtain: it sets the boundary between public performance and disorder.
nuance.etymology: From Latin decorum, 'that which is proper', neuter of decorus.
common_mistakes: Using 'decorum' for everyday manners where 'manners' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle as 'DEK-or-um'; the first syllable is 'dih'.

senses.definition: To delay or postpone.
senses.example: We're going to defer the decision until we have all the facts.

senses.definition: To postpone induction into military service.
senses.example: He chose to defer his draft notice while he finished his graduate degree.

senses.definition: After winning the opening coin toss, to postpone until the start of the second half a team's choice of whether to kick off or receive (and to allow the opposing team to make this choice at the start of the first half).
senses.example: After winning the coin toss, our coach chose to defer the kickoff choice to halftime.

senses.definition: To delay, to wait.
senses.example: The judge decided to defer the ruling until more evidence came in.

senses.definition: To submit to the opinion or desire of others in respect to their judgment or authority.
senses.example: Although I'm the older sibling, I usually defer to my sister on travel plans.

senses.definition: To render, to offer.
senses.example: Pilgrims came to the shrine to defer their respects to the aging abbot.

core.definition: To put something off to a later time, or to yield to someone's judgment or authority out of respect.

pronunciation.tip: One stressed syllable with the r-colored vowel of 'fur'. Don't add a second syllable or a hard 'd' at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Deferring a decision is practical, but deferring to someone can sound respectful or submissive depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'defer to' someone's expertise or judgment in meetings, and 'defer' a payment, meeting, or decision when delaying it. In university and finance, 'defer' is common for postponing enrollment or loan payments. Do not confuse it with 'refer', which means to send someone elsewhere or mention something.

distinctions.note: Postpone is a general and common word for delaying; defer is more formal and often used for payments, decisions, or admissions.
Refer means to send someone elsewhere or mention something; defer means to delay or yield to someone's judgment.

examples.everyday: Let's defer the decision about dinner until everyone is off work.
examples.professional: I'd like to defer the rollout to next quarter so the data team can finish validation.
examples.analytical: Scholars who defer to tradition without argument risk confusing authority with truth.

nuance.analogy: Like putting a letter in a drawer for later: the task still exists, but it waits.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English deferren, from Latin differre 'to carry apart, delay', and in the sense of yielding, from Latin deferre 'to bring down, submit'.
common_mistakes: Confusing defer with refer: 'I deferred him to the manager' is wrong; say 'I referred him to the manager'.
Using 'defer to' with a noun meaning postponement; 'defer to' means yield to, so say 'defer the meeting' for postponing.

defer.etymology: Originally a variant of; from Middle English *differren* (“to postpone”), from Old French *differer*, from Latin *differō*.

senses.definition: To change the form of (something), usually thus making it disordered or irregular; to give (something) an abnormal or unusual shape.
senses.example: a face deformed by bitterness

senses.definition: To change the look of (something), usually thus making it imperfect or unattractive; to give (something) an abnormal or unusual appearance.
senses.example: a face deformed by bitterness

senses.definition: To mar the character or quality of (something).
senses.example: a marriage deformed by jealousy

senses.definition: To become changed in shape or misshapen.
To alter the shape of (something) by applying a force or stress.
senses.example: Heat from the sun can deform the plastic lids if they sit on the dashboard.

core.definition: To change the shape of something, usually by bending, twisting or pressing it so it is no longer normal or regular.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, FORM. The first syllable is a weak 'dih', not 'dee'. The r is clearly pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it usually implies damage or loss of normal shape.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deform most often for physical objects, such as metal, plastic or structures, and in engineering reports. In everyday speech people more often say 'bent', 'warped' or 'crushed'. Using deform for a person's body is considered insensitive, so Americans avoid it in that context.

distinctions.note: Distort usually refers to twisting a shape, image or meaning so it is misleading, while deform focuses on a physical change in form.
Warp usually refers to bending flat things, like wood or records, because of heat or moisture, while deform covers any physical change in shape.

examples.everyday: Don't leave that plastic water bottle in the car, because it will deform in the heat.
examples.professional: The bracket began to deform under the load, so we need to increase the wall thickness before the next test.
examples.analytical: A theory that bends its evidence to fit its conclusions risks deforming the very reasoning it claims to protect.

nuance.analogy: Like soft clay pressed flat by a thumb, the shape is changed and may not spring back.
nuance.etymology: From Latin deformare, from de- 'away' and forma 'shape'.
common_mistakes: Using deform for people's bodies, which sounds offensive in American English.
Confusing the verb deform with the adjective deformed, as in 'it was deform' instead of 'it was deformed'.

deform.etymology: From Middle English *deforme* (“out of shape, deformed”), from Middle French *deforme*, or directly from its etymon Latin *dēfōrmis* (“departing physically from the correct shape, deformed, malformed, misshapen, ugly; departing morally from the correct…

senses.definition: Able to be delivered.
senses.example: The packages were not deliverable because the roads had flooded out.

senses.definition: The tangible end product; that which will be delivered.
senses.example: Due to inclement weather, we will be unable to provide our deliverables.

core.definition: A specific product, document, or result that a project or contract requires a team to hand over by a set date.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LIV, the second syllable. The -er- is a reduced American 'r' vowel, and the final -able is weak, so say it as 'uh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American offices, deliverable is a standard meeting and project-management word, used constantly in status updates and sprint planning. Saying what the deliverables are for a week is normal. In casual talk it can sound corporate, so use it at work rather than with friends.

distinctions.note: A milestone is a point in time marking progress, while a deliverable is the concrete item produced at or by that point.
Output is a general word for what a process produces, while a deliverable is specifically something agreed in advance and owed to a client or stakeholder.

examples.everyday: My manager is on my case about the deliverables for the quarter, so I'm working late tonight.
examples.professional: The main deliverables for this sprint are the updated dashboard, the data validation report, and the model documentation.
examples.analytical: A useful framework separates outcomes from deliverables, since a deliverable can be completed without producing the outcome it was meant to serve.

nuance.analogy: A deliverable is like a package with a shipping label: it has a name, a due date, and a recipient waiting for it.
nuance.etymology: From deliver (from Latin liberare, to set free) plus -able, meaning able to be handed over.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in dih-liv-er-ABLE.
Using deliverable only for physical goods; in projects it often means a report, code, or document.

conversation.text: The main deliverable is a report with our recommendations.
Can we list all the deliverables and their due dates?
The client is expecting the first deliverable next Tuesday.

senses.definition: The conveyance or transfer of an estate, either in fee for life or for years, most commonly the latter.
senses.example: The landlord's demise of the property to the tenant was recorded for a term of ninety-nine years.

senses.definition: Transmission by formal act or conveyance to an heir or successor; transference; especially, the transfer or transmission of the crown or royal authority to a successor.
senses.example: The demise of the crown passed authority to the prince without any public ceremony.

senses.definition: Death; decease.
The end of something, in a negative sense; downfall.
senses.example: The lack of funding ultimately led to the project's demise.

senses.definition: The atmospheric disintegration of a satellite or satellite component upon re-entering Earth's atmosphere.
senses.example: Relocating components to places where they receive more heating effect earlier in the reentry and even triggering a partial break-up of the satellite structure during reentry to aid demise.

senses.definition: To convey, as by will or lease.
senses.example: The landlord demised the cottage to her nephew for the remainder of his life.

senses.definition: To transmit by inheritance.
senses.example: The old farm was demised to the eldest son under the terms of the will.

senses.definition: To pass by inheritance.
senses.example: The estate demised to her son when the probate court approved the will.

senses.definition: To die.
senses.example: Poor old Uncle Walter demised in his sleep, God rest his soul.

core.definition: The end of something, such as a company, institution, or custom, or formally, a person's death.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MYZE. The final s is a z sound, so the word rhymes with rise or prize, not with Denise.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually describes a decline or ending that is regretted or significant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use demise in news, business, and reports, for example the demise of a company or an industry. For a death it sounds formal, so in conversation most people would say passed away or died. It can be used lightly in writing to describe a dramatic end, but not for minor losses.

distinctions.note: Death is the plain, universal word, while demise is a formal or journalistic term that often focuses on the end of a role, institution, or organization.
Collapse suggests a sudden fall or breakdown, while demise can describe a slower and more general end.

examples.everyday: Some of my friends were sad about the demise of our favorite diner when it closed last year.
examples.professional: The report links the demise of the legacy software to a lack of investment in cloud infrastructure.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the demise of the old moral order was less sudden than many historians have claimed.

nuance.analogy: The demise of an institution is like a tree that slowly loses its leaves and then falls, rather than one that is cut down in an instant.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French demis, past participle of desmettre, to dismiss or transfer, from Latin dimittere.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as s instead of z.
Using demise for ordinary, minor endings, which sounds exaggerated.

demise.etymology: From Middle English *demyse*, *dimise*, *dimisse*, *dymyse*, from Middle French *démise*, the feminine singular past participle of *démettre* (“to put down, relinquish”); from Latin *dēmissa*, feminine singular of perfect passive participle of *dēmittō*.

senses.definition: To press down.
senses.example: Depress the upper lever to start the machine.

senses.definition: To make depressed, sad or bored.
senses.example: Winter depresses me.

senses.definition: To cause a depression or a decrease in parts of the economy.
senses.example: Lower productivity will eventually depress wages.

senses.definition: To bring down or humble; to abase (pride, etc.).
senses.example: The preacher warned that pride would depress even the most accomplished man before God.

senses.definition: To reduce (an equation) in a lower degree.
senses.example: To solve the cubic, we depress the equation by eliminating the quadratic term first.

core.definition: To make someone feel sad, discouraged, or hopeless; also to press something down.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, and the final s is a clear /s/ sound. Do not add a vowel after the final s or stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing a lowering of mood or activity
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, depress usually describes a bad effect on mood, as in the news depresses me. People also say that a rainy week is depressing. The word also appears in economics, where a slowdown depresses prices or wages. To describe a clinical condition, Americans use depression or depressed in most contexts.

distinctions.note: Discourage means to make someone lose confidence or willingness to act, while depress often refers to a deeper or more general lowering of mood or activity.
Sadden focuses on causing sorrow, while depress can also mean lowering prices, wages, or activity.

examples.everyday: That gray weather really depresses me this time of year.
examples.professional: The recent price cuts are depressing margins across the whole product line.
examples.analytical: Certain philosophers argued that anxious habits of thought tend to depress the mind's capacity for joy.

nuance.analogy: Like pressing down on a spring, depress pushes a mood, price, or activity down below its normal level.
nuance.etymology: From Latin deprimere, 'to press down', from de- 'down' plus premere 'to press'.
common_mistakes: Using depress as a noun for the clinical illness; say depression.
Saying I am depress instead of I am depressed.

depress.etymology: From Middle English *depressen*, from Old French *depresser*, from Latin *dēpressus*, perfect participle of *dēprimō* (“to press down, to weigh down”), from *dē-* + *premō*.

senses.definition: Liable to destruction; capable of being destroyed.

core.definition: Able to be destroyed or broken; capable of being damaged, ruined, or taken apart by force.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, -STRUHK-, and the last syllable is a light 'buhl', with the l sounding like a syllable. Learners often stress the final syllable or pronounce the middle vowel too strongly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a physical or digital property, such as an object in a video game or a material in engineering.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use destructible in engineering, game design, and science when describing whether something can be broken. In casual speech, people more often say 'can break' or 'can be destroyed.' The opposite, indestructible, is more common in everyday talk for something very durable.

distinctions.note: Destructible is the standard and more common word in technical and game contexts, while destroyable is less standard and rarely used in formal writing.
Fragile means easily broken, while destructible means it can be destroyed in general, without necessarily being delicate.

examples.everyday: The kids' sand castle is destructible, so they can smash it down and build it again.
examples.professional: Make the wall destructible in the game engine so players can blast through it during the demo.
examples.analytical: Philosophers distinguish a destructible object, which can be broken, from a thing that is indestructible by its very nature.

nuance.analogy: A destructible object is like a sandcastle: it looks solid, but a wave or a child can wipe it away.
nuance.etymology: From Latin destructibilis, from destruere, meaning to pull down.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, saying 'dih-struk-TIH-buhl' instead of 'dih-STRUHK-tih-buhl'.
Confusing destructible with destructive, which describes something that causes destruction rather than something that can be destroyed.

core.definition: Old Testament books, such as Tobit and Wisdom, accepted as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches but placed in the Apocrypha by most Protestants.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on NAH in 'canonical', with secondary stress on 'doo'. Say 'doo' not 'dyoo', and make 'books' with the short 'oo' of 'put'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a term, though the choice of word signals a tradition: Catholics and Orthodox say 'deuterocanonical', while many Protestants say 'Apocrypha'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in theology, biblical studies and church history. It means 'second canon', since these books were recognized after the others. The list differs by tradition.

distinctions.note: Apocrypha is the usual Protestant label for these books, implying they are not Scripture but may be useful reading.
Protocanonical books are those accepted in the Hebrew Bible and by all Christians.
Pseudepigrapha are ancient writings falsely attributed to biblical figures and are not part of any major Christian canon.

examples.everyday: My Catholic friend's Bible has Tobit and Wisdom, and she told me those are the deuterocanonical books.
examples.professional: In my seminar, I will compare how different churches treat the deuterocanonical books in their lectionaries.
examples.analytical: Whether the deuterocanonical books belong to the Old Testament depends on whether one follows the Septuagint tradition of the early church or the Hebrew canon later fixed in Judaism.

nuance.analogy: Like a second set of chapters added later to a shared family history, which some branches keep and others set aside.
nuance.etymology: From Greek deuteros, 'second', + kanonikos, 'according to the rule'; coined in the 16th century.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the beginning as 'dyoo' instead of 'doo'.
Treating it as a synonym for Apocrypha without noting that it signals acceptance as canon.
Stressing the first syllable instead of NAH.
nuance.biblical_note: These books include Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch, and 1 and 2 Maccabees, plus additions to Esther and Daniel. They are not in the Hebrew Bible but appear in the Greek Septuagint. The RSV places them in the Apocrypha section of its expanded edition; the New Testament never quotes them explicitly as Scripture, though some echoes are claimed.

traditions.view: The Orthodox Church receives these books, and some others, as part of the Old Testament in the Septuagint tradition, used in worship. The exact list varies slightly among Orthodox churches.
The Council of Trent in 1546 defined them as canonical Scripture, so Catholic Bibles include seven additional books plus additions to Esther and Daniel.

Most Protestants follow the Hebrew canon and place these books in the Apocrypha, valuable for reading but not for establishing doctrine. Anglicans read them for example of life and manners, and Lutherans include them in some Bibles as useful but not Scripture.

senses.definition: Resembling a devil.
senses.example: The painting showed a devilish creature with horns and blazing red eyes.

senses.definition: Evil, wicked.
Roguish or mischievous.
senses.example: a devilish grin

senses.definition: Excessive, extreme.
senses.example: A devilish effort yielded a devilish success.

senses.definition: Devilishly; very; exceedingly.
senses.example: It was devilish hot outside today.

core.definition: Wicked or evil, or playfully mischievous; also used as an adverb meaning very or exceedingly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, so say DEV-lish, and do not stress the final -ish.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or playful; it can describe real wickedness, but more often a teasing grin or a sly, mischievous charm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say devilish about a sly smile, a prank, or a tempting dessert ('a devilish grin', 'devilishly good brownies'). Used with intensifying force, devilishly means very, as in 'devilishly hot today'. For serious evil, Americans usually choose wicked or diabolical.

distinctions.note: Wicked is stronger and more morally serious; devilish is lighter and often playful.
Diabolical is formal and suggests deliberate, extreme evil, while devilish is casual.

examples.everyday: He gave me a devilish grin and then ate the last cookie.
examples.professional: The product team's devilish bug only appeared when two users edited the same file.
examples.analytical: Milton's Satan is devilish not merely in deed but in the seductive rhetoric he uses to tempt Eve.

nuance.analogy: A devilish smile is like a cat that has just knocked a glass off the table and looks pleased about it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'devel', from Old English 'deofol', from Late Latin 'diabolus', from Greek 'diabolos' meaning slanderer.
common_mistakes: Using devilish only for literal devils and missing its playful sense.
Stressing the final syllable as in devil-ISH.

senses.definition: A rolling down.
A descent, especially one that passes through a series of revolutions, or by succession.
The transference of a right to a successor, or of a power from one body to another.
Degeneration.
senses.example: It is quite disheartening to witness the devolution of our nation's political discourse over the past several years.

senses.definition: The transfer of some powers and the delegation of some functions from a central government to local government (e.g. from the U.K. parliament to Scottish parliament and Welsh assembly).
senses.example: The question of whether England should receive devolution like Scotland and Wales have has dogged British politics for years.

core.definition: The transfer of power or authority from a central government to regional or local bodies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, 'LOO', not the 'vo' syllable. The final -tion is pronounced 'shun'. Learners often put the stress on 'DEV' or misplace it as 'dev-uh-loo-SHUN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes an administrative or political process without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, devolution appears mostly in political science, policy debates, and discussions of federalism, often with reference to power shifting to states, counties, or territories. Americans sometimes say 'decentralization' or 'delegation of power' instead. Outside politics, the word can also mean gradual decline, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Decentralization is a broader term for spreading power or operations away from a center; devolution specifically means authority formally passed to lower bodies.
Secession means breaking away from a state entirely; devolution keeps power within the larger political system.
Evolution means gradual development or change over time; devolution often means gradual transfer of power, or sometimes decline, so the words are not interchangeable.

examples.everyday: My friend says the devolution of school funding to our state has changed how our district spends money.
examples.professional: The devolution of budgeting authority to regional managers cut our approval times in half last year.
examples.analytical: Devolution raises a basic question: whether authority delegated by a central government can later be reclaimed without a constitutional change.

nuance.analogy: Devolution is like a parent handing the car keys to a teenager: the authority still comes from the family, but the decisions are made closer to the road.
nuance.etymology: From Latin devolutio, from devolvere, to roll down, from de- (down) plus volvere (to roll).
common_mistakes: Confusing devolution with evolution, which is a different word with a different meaning.
Putting the main stress on 'vo' instead of 'lu' as in 'dev-OH-lu-shun'.

devolution.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *dévolution*, from Medieval Latin *devolutio*, from Latin *devolvo*.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to dimensions.
Having dimension or dimensions; three-dimensional.
senses.example: The architect sketched a dimensional model of the building before choosing any materials.

senses.definition: Appended to cardinal numbers or algebraic symbols to form adjectives meaning "having the stated number of dimensions".
senses.example: Physicists often describe spacetime as a four-dimensional continuum rather than three dimensions plus time.

senses.definition: Pertaining to dimensional lumber: having a standardized, nominal width and depth, which may differ from the actual width and depth.
senses.example: dimensional boards, dimensional sizes, dimensional wood

core.definition: Relating to the measurable extent of an object or space, or to the number of dimensions in a space, as in dimensional analysis.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MEN. The '-sion' is pronounced 'shun', and the final '-al' is a weak 'ul'. Do not say 'DIE-men-shun-al' with the stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes measurement or structure without emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dimensional mostly in science, engineering, design and manufacturing. In everyday speech, people say 'three-dimensional' or '3D' instead. The phrase 'dimensional specs' is common in carpentry and product design, so ask for the dimensional measurements if you need the exact size.

distinctions.note: Spatial refers to space and position, while dimensional refers to measurable extent or the number of dimensions.
Three-dimensional is the everyday phrase for a solid object; dimensional is more technical and often appears in analysis.

examples.everyday: Ask the carpenter for the exact dimensional specs before we order the cabinets, so they fit the wall.
examples.professional: Before we sign off on the model, let's run a dimensional analysis on the pressure equation to catch unit errors.
examples.analytical: Dimensional analysis constrains physical laws: any valid equation must balance its units, which is why the theorem can reduce the number of variables.

nuance.analogy: Like a map scale: the drawing is only useful if its measurements match the real object.
nuance.etymology: From dimension, from Latin dimensio 'a measuring out', from dimetiri 'to measure out'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'DIE-men-shun'; the main stress is on MEN.
Saying 'a dimensional model' in casual speech where Americans say 'a three-dimensional model'.

senses.definition: A typically small restaurant, historically modeled after a railroad dining car, that serves lower-class fare, normally having a counter with stools along one side and booths on the other.
senses.example: We grabbed a booth at the old diner on Route 9 and ordered pancakes.

senses.definition: Someone who dines.
senses.example: As a generous diner, he always insisted on ordering the most expensive wine.

senses.definition: A car in a railroad train that serves meals.
senses.example: The train's diner served eggs and coffee until the last stop in Chicago.

senses.definition: A commemorative currency of Andorra, not legal tender, divided into 100 centims.
senses.example: The shop sold a commemorative diner, though shopkeepers wouldn't accept it as payment.

senses.definition: (rare) Someone who gives a dinner.
senses.example: Grandma was a gracious diner, always hosting Sunday dinners for the whole family.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A small, casual restaurant, often with a long counter with stools and booths along the walls, serving simple, inexpensive food.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the r is pronounced clearly, as a rhotic American r. Do not add an extra syllable between the n and the r.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. A diner suggests comfort, affordability and nostalgia rather than fine dining.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use diner for a casual, usually family-run restaurant that serves breakfast all day, burgers, pancakes and coffee. You can say 'Let's grab a bite at the diner' with friends or family. Diner is not used for fancy restaurants, which Americans call a restaurant or bistro.

distinctions.note: Restaurant is the general word for any place that serves meals, while diner suggests a casual, informal, often retro place.
A cafe mainly serves coffee, tea and light food, while a diner serves full meals such as breakfast, sandwiches and dinner plates.

examples.everyday: Let's grab pancakes at that diner on Main Street before the game.
examples.professional: After the client meeting, our team stopped at a diner near the office for a quick lunch.
examples.analytical: The American diner, with its counter and booths, has become a symbol of mid-century national identity and small-town hospitality.

nuance.analogy: A diner is like a friendly neighborhood kitchen opened to the public, with no formalities.
nuance.etymology: From dine (to eat a meal) plus the suffix -er, meaning one who dines.
common_mistakes: Saying 'diner' for any restaurant, when Americans use it mainly for casual places.
Pronouncing it as 'dine-ER' with a stressed second syllable.

conversation.text: Let's get breakfast at the diner on the corner; it's open twenty-four hours.
This diner makes the best milkshakes and fries in town.
The restaurant was full of diners, and the kitchen was slammed.

senses.definition: Ruffled; upset and embarrassed.
senses.example: The disconcerted student lost his place in the speech and stared at the floor.

senses.definition: Self-consciously distressed.
senses.example: He felt disconcerted when everyone turned to watch him trip on the stairs.

senses.definition: Frustrated and disarranged.
senses.example: The disconcerted accountant stared at the ledger, where every column refused to balance.

core.definition: Upset, unsettled, or thrown off balance, usually by something unexpected or awkward.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -SUR-, the second part of the verb disconcert. The r is strongly colored, and the final -ed is weak, sounding like 'id'. Do not stress the first syllable as in DIS-kun-surt.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; it describes being unsettled, often with a hint of embarrassment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disconcerted for someone who is unsettled or embarrassed, often by a surprise or a rude remark. It is more formal than rattled or thrown, and it appears often in news and writing. In conversation people usually say 'I was kind of thrown' or 'that threw me off'. A natural reply to someone who seems unsettled is 'I can see why that would throw you.'

distinctions.note: Unsettled is more general and can describe a mood, a place, or a situation; disconcerted refers to a person who has been surprised or embarrassed.
Rattled is informal and suggests losing your nerve; disconcerted is more polite and a bit more formal.

examples.everyday: She looked a little disconcerted when the waiter remembered her order from last year.
examples.professional: The client seemed disconcerted by the sudden change in the model's results, so we walked through the assumptions again.
examples.analytical: The reader is left disconcerted, not by any single claim, but by the way the author quietly undermines her own certainty.

nuance.analogy: Like an actor who forgets a line in front of an audience and has to recover without missing a beat.
nuance.etymology: From French déconcerter, from dis- (undoing) plus concerter (to arrange together).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with disconnected or discontented; disconcerted means upset by surprise, not separated or generally unhappy.
Using the wrong preposition: say disconcerted by something, not disconcerted from something.

senses.definition: Any abnormal or harmful condition, as of society, people's attitudes, way of living etc.
senses.example: Many scholars argue that greed is a disease eating away at modern democracy.

senses.definition: A lack of ease; uneasiness; trouble; vexation; disquiet.
senses.example: He felt a strange disease in his heart whenever he walked past that house.

senses.definition: An abnormal condition of a human, animal or plant that causes discomfort or dysfunction; distinct from injury insofar as the latter is usually instantaneously acquired.
senses.example: The tomato plants had some kind of disease that left their leaves splotchy and their fruit withered.

senses.definition: To infect with a disease.
senses.example: Contaminated water can disease whole villages if nobody boils it first.

core.definition: An illness or medical condition that harms the body or mind, such as diabetes, influenza or heart disease.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable (dih-ZEEZ). The final s is voiced like z, so it does not sound like dis-EASE with an s at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names something serious and harmful, so it sounds more clinical or grave than sick.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disease for specific medical conditions and in health discussions. For everyday illnesses such as a cold, people say 'I'm sick' or 'I've got a bug.' Disease sounds more serious and is common in doctor's offices, news and public health.

distinctions.note: Illness is how you feel when unwell; disease is the medical condition that causes it.
Sickness is a general word for being ill and is more everyday; disease is more specific and clinical.
Disorder is broader and often used for mental or functional problems; disease usually refers to a defined biological condition.

examples.everyday: My mom has a chronic disease, so she checks her blood sugar every morning before breakfast.
examples.professional: The model flags patients at risk for cardiovascular disease using data from routine lab work.
examples.analytical: A disease is not simply a deviation from the norm; its definition depends on values about what counts as a healthy human life.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire in the walls of a house: the damage spreads quietly until someone finds the source.
nuance.etymology: From Old French desaise, discomfort, from des- (lack of) and aise (ease).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final s as an s sound instead of z.
Calling a minor cold a disease, which sounds exaggerated in everyday talk.

disease.etymology: From Middle English *disese*, from Anglo-Norman *desese*, from Old French *desaise*, from *des-* + *aise*.

senses.definition: In a disloyal manner.

core.definition: In a way that shows a lack of loyalty, such as betraying someone or supporting an opponent.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LOY, as in disloyal. The last syllable is a reduced 'ly' sound, pronounced 'lee', with only one l sound.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes an action performed in a way that betrays trust.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use disloyally in everyday speech. They usually say 'betrayed us' or 'turned on us' instead. You will see it in formal writing, history, political commentary or literature, where the adverb describes a specific act of betrayal.

distinctions.note: Treacherously stresses deceit and danger; disloyally stresses a failure of commitment or allegiance.
Unfaithfully usually refers to romantic partners or religious faith; disloyally fits groups, causes, friends and countries.

examples.professional: He spoke disloyally about the company in the press interview, which is why his contract was not renewed.
examples.analytical: Historians note that the general acted disloyally toward his government, yet his motives remain debated in the sources.

nuance.analogy: Like a team captain who leaves the field in the middle of the game and joins the other side: the action itself is what matters.
nuance.etymology: From disloyal, plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Middle English.
common_mistakes: Using 'disloyally' as a casual word for 'unfairly'; it means in a way that breaks loyalty.
Saying 'disloyal' as an adverb without -ly, as in 'he acted disloyal'.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'lee' with a second clear l, as in 'dis-LOY-uh-lly'.

senses.definition: Inclined, minded.
Having a certain disposition.
senses.example: well-disposed; ill-disposed

core.definition: Inclined or willing to do something; having a certain attitude or tendency toward someone or something.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -POSE-, with a long 'oh' vowel. The ending is pronounced as a voiced z followed by a d sound, so it is not 'dis-POSED' with a hard s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can describe willingness or a general attitude, positive or negative depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use 'disposed' in set phrases such as 'disposed to help', 'well disposed toward', or 'not disposed to agree'. In casual talk, 'inclined', 'in the mood', or 'willing' sound more natural. The word fits formal writing, professional advice, or polite refusals.

distinctions.note: Inclined is the more everyday word for a leaning or tendency, while disposed is more formal and can describe a settled attitude.
Willing means ready to do something when asked, while disposed suggests an underlying inclination or mood.
Prone means likely to experience something, usually something bad, as in prone to errors, while disposed refers to attitude or willingness.

examples.everyday: I'm not really disposed to go out tonight, so let's just order in.
examples.professional: The board seems disposed to approve the budget if we can show lower travel costs.
examples.analytical: Hume's skeptic is disposed to suspend judgment rather than assert a causal connection that cannot be observed.

nuance.analogy: Being disposed to something is like a door already tilted slightly open: it moves easily in one direction.
nuance.etymology: From dispose, from Latin disponere, 'to arrange' or 'set in order'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'disposed to' with 'disposed of', which means got rid of something.
Using 'disposed' where 'inclined' is more natural in casual speech.

senses.definition: To deprive someone of the possession of land, especially by evicting them.
To deprive someone of possession in general.
senses.example: The eviction notice threatened to dispossess the family of their home and savings.

senses.definition: To take possession of the ball/puck etc. (from someone).

core.definition: To take away someone's property, land, or possession, often by legal force or eviction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'ZES', the third syllable. Don't pronounce the 's' in the middle as a 'z'; it is an 's' sound before the stressed syllable's 'es'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes an unjust or harmful taking away of property or rights.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'dispossess' mainly in news, history, and legal contexts, often about evictions or land seizures. In everyday speech, people would more often say 'kick out' or 'evict.' The verb usually takes 'of' before the thing taken, as in 'dispossessed of their land.'

distinctions.note: 'Evict' refers specifically to removing a tenant from a home; 'dispossess' is broader and covers land or property.
'Deprive' means to take away something needed or wanted; 'dispossess' focuses on losing ownership.

examples.everyday: My neighbor felt dispossessed when the landlord sold the building.
examples.professional: The contract was challenged because the company tried to dispossess the subcontractor of its equipment.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that colonial policy dispossessed indigenous communities of their ancestral land.

nuance.analogy: To dispossess someone is like taking a book from a child's hands: the object leaves their control.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'dis-' (apart) plus 'possess,' from 'possidere,' to hold.
common_mistakes: Using 'dispossess' without 'of' before the object.
Confusing it with 'repossess,' which means to take back goods for nonpayment.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible the idea appears in discussions of land taken from one people and given to another, such as the Israelites taking the land of Canaan. The Hebrew word 'yarash' means to take possession or inherit. Relevant passages include Deuteronomy 9:4-5, which says Israel will not enter the land because of its own righteousness but because the nations are being driven out; Numbers 33:53, which commands Israel to take possession of the land; and Joshua 23:5, which promises that God will drive out the nations before them.

dispossess.etymology: From Middle English, from Middle French *despossesser*.

senses.definition: The process of resolving disputes between parties.

core.definition: The process of settling a disagreement between parties, often through negotiation, mediation, or arbitration, rather than in court.

pronunciation.tip: In compounds, the first word takes the main stress, so say DIS-pyoot with the stress on the first syllable. The second word's stress is on LOO, and the ending -tion is shun, not shn.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a process, not a conflict.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dispute resolution mainly in law, business, human resources, and contract negotiations. The abbreviation ADR, for alternative dispute resolution, is common in legal and corporate settings. In everyday life, people say 'work it out' or 'settle it,' so the phrase can sound formal in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Conflict resolution is broader and covers personal, social, and international conflicts; dispute resolution usually refers to a formal disagreement between parties.
Mediation is one specific method of dispute resolution, in which a neutral person helps the parties reach an agreement.
Arbitration is another method in which a neutral third party makes a binding decision, unlike mediation, which does not impose one.

examples.everyday: We tried a neighborhood mediator for the fence dispute, which was a good form of dispute resolution and saved us a lawsuit.
examples.professional: Our contract includes a dispute resolution clause that requires arbitration before either side files a lawsuit.
examples.analytical: Effective dispute resolution depends less on who is right than on whether both parties accept the procedure as legitimate.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who doesn't pick a team but makes sure the game ends with a fair result that both players accept.
nuance.etymology: Dispute from Latin disputare 'to argue'; resolution from Latin resolutio 'a loosening, untying'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'dispute solution' instead of dispute resolution, which is the standard term.
Placing the stress on resolution (reh-zuh-LOO-shuhn) without stressing DIS-pyoot in the first word.

senses.definition: An amount of space between points (often geographical points), usually (but not necessarily) measured along a straight line.
senses.example: angular distance focal distance

senses.definition: Chiefly in from a distance: a place which is far away or remote; specifically, a more remote part of a landscape or view as contrasted with the foreground.
senses.example: Seen from a distance, the mountains looked like a thin blue line.

senses.definition: Chiefly with a modifying word: a measure between two points or quantities; a difference, a variance.
senses.example: angular distance focal distance

senses.definition: An interval or length of time between events.
senses.example: The distance in years between his two marriages surprised everyone at the reunion.

senses.definition: A separation in some way other than space or time.
senses.example: The friendship did not survive the row: they kept each other at a distance.

senses.definition: Synonym of length (“an extent measured along the longest dimension of an object”).
senses.example: Measure the distance from the bottom of the door to the floor.

senses.definition: A disagreement, a dispute; also, an estrangement.
senses.example: Their argument over the inheritance created a distance between the two brothers.

senses.definition: The amount of space between points (often geographical points), usually (but not necessarily) measured along a straight line.
senses.example: The distance to Petersborough is thirty miles.

senses.definition: The maximum amount of space between a boxer and their opponent within which the boxer can punch effectively.
senses.example: The boxer stayed at distance, waiting for an opening before throwing her jab.

senses.definition: Often in go the distance, last the distance, or stay the distance: the scheduled duration of a bout.
senses.example: Her knee was hurting, but she was determined to go the distance.

senses.definition: The amount of space between a fencer and their opponent, which the fencer tries to control in order to gain an advantage over the opponent.
senses.example: The fencer retreated a step to regain the distance she had lost.

senses.definition: Originally, the space measured back from the winning post which a racehorse running in a heat must reach when the winner has covered the whole course, in order to run in a subsequent heat; also, the point on the racecourse that space away from the winning post; now, the point on a racecourse 240 yards from the winning post.
senses.example: The stewards ruled that the horse had not reached the distance and could not run again.

senses.definition: The complete length of a course over which a race is run.
senses.example: The race distance is 26.2 miles, so pace yourself from the start.

senses.definition: Chiefly preceded by the, especially in into or in the distance: the place that is far away or remote.
senses.example: In the distance, a train whistle echoed across the empty prairie.

senses.definition: The state of being separated from something else, especially by a long way; the state of being far off or remote; farness, remoteness.
The entire amount of progress to an objective.
senses.example: He had promised to perform this task, but did not go the distance.

senses.definition: The state of remoteness or separation in some way other than space or time.
senses.example: the distance between a descendant and their ancestor

senses.definition: The state of people not being close, friendly, or intimate with each other; also, the state of people who were once close, friendly, or intimate with each other no longer being so; estrangement.
Excessive reserve or lack of friendliness shown by a person; aloofness, coldness.
senses.example: She treated the new coworkers with a polite distance that discouraged friendship.

senses.definition: The rank to which an important person belongs.
senses.example: Clerks bowed low, sensing the distance of rank between themselves and the visiting duke.

senses.definition: The state of disagreement or dispute between people; dissension.
senses.example: The distance between the two factions grew after the vote, splitting the congregation.

senses.definition: Often followed by to or towards: an attitude of remoteness or reserve which respect requires; hence, ceremoniousness.
senses.example: He spoke to the elderly bishop with a respectful distance that everyone admired.

senses.definition: A difference in pitch between sounds; an interval.
senses.example: The distance between the two notes was a perfect fifth, which sounded pleasantly open.

senses.definition: The amount of space between soldiers or cavalry riders marching or standing in a rank; also, the amount of space between such ranks.
senses.example: The sergeant ordered the recruits to keep proper distance between ranks while marching.

senses.definition: Often followed by from: to set (someone or something) at a distance (noun sense 1.1) from someone or something else.
To cause (a place, a thing, etc.) to seem distant, or unfamiliar.
To leave behind (someone or something moving in the same direction; specifically, other competitors in a race) some distance away; to outpace, to outstrip.
To keep (someone) emotionally or socially apart from another person or people.
To exceed or surpass (someone, such as a peer or rival); to outdo, to outstrip.
To keep (oneself) away from someone or something, especially because one does not want to be associated with that person or thing.
senses.example: He distanced himself from the comments made by some of his colleagues.

senses.definition: To cover the entire distance to (something).
To depart from (a place); to leave (a place) behind.
To indicate or measure the distance to (a place).
To set (two or more things) at regular distances from each other; to space, to space out.
Often followed by from.
To set oneself at a distance from someone or something else; to move away from someone or something.
To keep oneself emotionally or socially apart from another person or people; to keep one's distance.

core.definition: The amount of space between two points, usually measured along a straight line, whether between places or between objects.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle t is light and the last syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like DIS-tuns, not dis-TANSS.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is value-free and simply describes space or separation; the context gives it warmth or coldness, as in keep your distance versus close distance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use distance constantly in everyday talk about driving, walking and travel, often with a rough estimate such as a long distance or walking distance. In casual speech you may hear it as a question, like How far is it? rather than What is the distance? The word also carries social meaning: keeping your distance means staying emotionally or physically away from someone.

distinctions.note: Length describes the long dimension of an object, such as the length of a table, while distance describes the separation between two points or objects.
Range is the span between the limits of a set of values or a capacity, whereas distance is the physical or metaphorical gap between two points.
Space is a general or open area, often without a fixed measure, while distance is a specific separation between two named points.

examples.everyday: It's about a twenty-minute drive, so the distance isn't too bad.
examples.professional: Latency between the two regions goes up with distance, so we moved the cache closer to the users.
examples.analytical: Berkeley argued that we do not see distance directly but learn it through cues, which challenges the naive assumption that depth is simply given to sight.

nuance.analogy: Like the gap between two chairs in a room, measured from one edge to the other.
nuance.etymology: From Latin distantia, from distare 'to stand apart', from dis- 'apart' plus stare 'to stand'.
common_mistakes: Saying in distance instead of in the distance for something far away.
Pronouncing it dis-TANSS, with the stress on the second syllable.

distance.etymology: From Middle English *distance*, *distaunce*, *destance* (“disagreement, dispute; discrimination; armed conflict; hostility; trouble; space between two points; time interval”), from Anglo-Norman *distance*, *distaunce*, *destance*, Middle French *distance*,…

senses.definition: An act of distributing or state of being distributed.
senses.example: The even distribution of rainfall across the valley helped the crops thrive.

senses.definition: An apportionment by law (of funds, property).
senses.example: The will specified the distribution of the estate among the three children.

senses.definition: The process by which goods get to final consumers over a geographical market, including storing, selling, shipping and advertising.
senses.example: The company's distribution network moves coffee from roasters to grocery stores nationwide.

senses.definition: Anything distributed; portion; share.
senses.example: Each volunteer received a generous distribution of the donated winter coats.

senses.definition: The result of distributing; arrangement.
senses.example: The seating distribution at the wedding left the bride's cousins near the back.

senses.definition: The total number of something sold or delivered to the clients.
senses.example: The distribution of my little rock magazine is about 3,000.

senses.definition: The frequency of occurrence or extent of existence.
senses.example: Scientists studied the distribution of the rare frog across the mountain streams.

senses.definition: The apportionment of income or wealth in a population.
senses.example: The wealth distribution became extremely skewed in the kleptocracy.

senses.definition: The way in which a player's hand is divided in suits, or in which a particular suit is divided between the players.
senses.example: The declarer had 3-6-2-2 distribution.

senses.definition: A probability distribution; the set of relative likelihoods that a variable will have a value in a given interval.
senses.example: The sample means follow a normal distribution with a mean of zero.

senses.definition: A subset of the tangent bundle of a manifold that satisfies certain properties; used to construct the notions of integrability and foliation of a manifold.
senses.example: The Frobenius theorem says a distribution is integrable exactly when it is involutive.

senses.definition: A set of bundled software components.
senses.example: a Linux distribution

senses.definition: The process or result of the sale of securities, especially their placement among investors with long-term investment strategies.
senses.example: The bank managed the distribution of the new bonds to pension funds.

senses.definition: The resolution of a whole into its parts.
senses.example: Her analysis began with a distribution of the argument into its three core claims.

senses.definition: The steps or operations by which steam is supplied to and withdrawn from the cylinder at each stroke of the piston: admission, suppression or cutting off, release or exhaust, and compression of exhaust steam prior to the next admission.
senses.example: The engineer adjusted the valve gear to improve steam distribution in the cylinder.

senses.definition: A rhetorical technique in which a subject is divided into multiple cases based on some property or properties, and each case is addressed individually.
senses.example: In his sermon, the preacher used distribution to address the three types of sinners separately.

senses.definition: (historical) The process of sorting the types and placing them in their proper boxes in the cases.
senses.example: The apprentice spent the morning on distribution, returning loose type to its proper cases.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The act of sharing or spreading things among people or places, or the way something is spread out in a pattern.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on BYOO, the third syllable, and the final -tion is pronounced 'shun'. The stress shifts from distribute (dih-STRIB-yoot) to distribution, so do not keep the first stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a process or pattern, and it is positive or negative depending on the outcome, such as fair or unequal distribution.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'distribution' for goods reaching stores, for distributing food or aid, and in statistics for how data is spread. In everyday talk people often say 'who gets what' or 'how it is spread out' instead, but 'distribution' is clear in news and business. In statistics it is a technical term, so the context matters.

distinctions.note: Delivery means carrying something to a specific person or address; distribution means spreading items across many people or places.
Allocation is a formal decision to assign resources to a purpose; distribution is the broader act of spreading them out.

examples.everyday: The city is changing how food distribution works at the local shelters this year.
examples.professional: Marketing is responsible for distribution of the product, so we need to coordinate with the sales channel.
examples.analytical: The paper argues that the distribution of wealth reflects institutional rules rather than individual merit.

nuance.analogy: Like a mail carrier with a bag of letters: the job is getting each piece to the right place.
nuance.etymology: From Latin distributio, from distribuere, meaning to divide among.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'DIS-tri-bu-tion', which sounds unnatural.
Using 'distribution' for a single delivery; a single package is a 'delivery', not a distribution.
nuance.biblical_note: In the early church the believers shared their possessions so that distribution was made to each as any had need, as described in Acts. The idea of sharing goods among those in need is central to Christian charity. Acts 2:45 describes believers selling property and distributing it to all who had need, and Acts 4:35 repeats the practice in summary form.

distribution.etymology: From Old French *distribution*, from Latin *distributio*, from *distribuere* (“to distribute”), itself from *dis-* (“apart”) + *tribuere* (“to assign, allot”) (from *tribus*).

senses.definition: No longer in use.

core.definition: No longer used or in use; no longer employed for its original purpose, often because it has been replaced or closed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -YOOZD, and the ending is a /zd/ sound, so do not drop the final d. Say the 'yoo' sound clearly, not 'oo' alone.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a state of fact and carries no judgment, though it can suggest neglect when used of buildings or places.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'disused' for things like railway lines, mines, buildings, and wells that are no longer operating. In everyday speech many people say 'out of use' or 'not used anymore,' so 'disused' sounds a bit more written or official. It is not a synonym for 'broken,' since a disused object may still be in working order.

distinctions.note: Obsolete means replaced by something newer and better; disused only means not currently used, with no comparison to a replacement.
Abandoned implies that someone deliberately left something behind, often with neglect; disused says nothing about why it stopped being used.
Defunct is used mainly of organizations, companies, or things that have stopped functioning altogether, and it is more final than disused.

examples.everyday: We walked along a disused railway line that is now a bike path near our house.
examples.professional: The old server room is disused since the migration, so we can move the spare racks there.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the ritual became disused once the community no longer shared its theological assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Like a train track with the rails pulled up: the route is still visible, but no trains run on it.
nuance.etymology: From dis- (not) plus used, from Latin usus, use.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like the noun 'disuse' with an s sound at the end, /dɪsˈjus/
Using 'disused' to mean broken; a disused item may still work perfectly well

senses.definition: A person with poor judgment and taste; a foolish or silly person.
senses.example: Stocks Genius or Dot-Com Doofus? – Wired News

core.definition: A foolish or clueless person, used as a mild, playful insult.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, DOO. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like fuss without the s sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative but mild and humorous. It can hurt if used to someone's face, so it is safer among friends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use doofus jokingly among friends, family, or in sitcoms, often as you doofus or a total doofus. It is too childish for work, serious criticism, or strangers. A natural reply, if you are teased, is laughing and saying Hey, that's not nice!

distinctions.note: Idiot is harsher and more insulting, while doofus is milder and more comic.
Dork suggests awkward or nerdy behavior, while doofus suggests poor judgment or silliness.
A goof is a small mistake or a playful fool, while a doofus is a person who keeps being foolish.

examples.everyday: Don't be such a doofus, you left your keys on the roof of the car again.
examples.professional: I was a doofus and sent the wrong file to the client, so I'm sending a correction now.
examples.analytical: The word doofus carries a comic tone that softens the insult, which is why it survives in family comedy.

nuance.analogy: A doofus is like a cartoon sidekick who keeps tripping over his own feet.
common_mistakes: Using doofus in serious criticism at work, where it sounds childish and rude.
Pronouncing the second syllable as foos; it is a reduced us sound.

doofus.etymology: possibly an alteration of earlier *goofus* (first attested in the 1920s) due to influence from Scots *doof* (“simpleton”).

senses.definition: The horizontal piece of material at the threshold of a doorway; a doorstep.

core.definition: The horizontal piece of wood, metal or stone at the bottom of a doorway, where the door closes against the floor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress DOOR, and pronounce 'sill' with a short i, like 'sil,' rhyming with 'fill.' Do not add a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain construction term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say 'threshold' for this part of the doorway, especially in everyday speech and real estate. 'Doorsill' is understood and used in home repair and construction. Avoid confusing it with 'windowsill,' which is a different piece.

distinctions.note: The threshold is the more common American word for this strip; doorsill is a more specific, technical term for the same part.
A doorstep is the step outside the door, while the doorsill is the piece at the bottom of the doorway.
A windowsill is the ledge beneath a window; a doorsill is at the base of a doorway.

examples.everyday: Watch out for the doorsill, because it's a little higher than the floor and I always catch my foot on it.
examples.professional: The contractor will replace the damaged doorsill before we install the new exterior door.
examples.analytical: The doorsill marks a material boundary between outside and inside, and in architecture it often signals a change of level.

nuance.analogy: A doorsill is like a small curb between two rooms that you step over to cross.
nuance.etymology: From door and sill; sill comes from Old English syll, 'beam, base.'
common_mistakes: Confusing doorsill with doorstep; the doorstep is outside, while the doorsill is inside the doorway.
Spelling it as two words, 'door sill.'

senses.definition: A pin, or block, of wood or metal, fitting into holes in the abutting portions of two pieces, and being partly in one piece and partly in the other, to keep them in their proper relative position.
senses.example: He aligned the two boards and tapped a wooden dowel into the holes to join them.

senses.definition: A wooden rod, as one to make short pins from.
senses.example: The woodworker cut a dowel from a length of ash to make pins for the chair.

senses.definition: A piece of wood or similar material fitted into a surface not suitable for fastening so that other pieces may be fastened to it.
senses.example: He tapped a dowel into the crumbling plaster so the bracket had something to grip.

senses.definition: To fasten together with dowels.
senses.example: We doweled the table legs to the frame before gluing the joints.

senses.definition: To furnish with dowels.
senses.example: A cooper dowels pieces for the head of a cask.

core.definition: A small wooden or metal peg that fits into aligned holes in two pieces of material to join them and keep them in position.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DOW, which has the 'ow' diphthong from 'cow'. The second syllable is a weak, syllabic 'l' that is often reduced to 'uhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dowel mainly in woodworking, furniture assembly, cabinetry, and DIY projects. You will see dowel rods and dowel pins sold in hardware stores. Americans say 'wooden dowel' for wood, and 'dowel pin' usually refers to a metal pin used in machining.

distinctions.note: A pin is any small pointed rod. A dowel is a cylindrical peg designed to fit into matching holes and align two pieces.
A screw holds pieces together through threads. A dowel mainly aligns pieces and bears shear loads, often together with glue.

examples.everyday: I need a dowel to fix the wobbly leg on this chair.
examples.professional: Use three dowels per joint so the cabinet frames line up cleanly during glue-up.
examples.analytical: The dowel acts as a mechanical guide, so the joint's strength depends on the fit of the hole and the grain direction.

nuance.analogy: A dowel is like a bridge pin between two planks, keeping them lined up at the right angle.
nuance.etymology: Possibly from Middle Low German or Dutch dovel, meaning a peg or plug.
common_mistakes: Saying it as DOE-wel with a long o and a separate syllable; it is two syllables, DOW-uhl.
Confusing it with 'dower' or 'dowry', which sound similar but are unrelated in meaning.

dowel.etymology: From Middle English *dowle*, *dule*, of uncertain origin.

senses.definition: To last too long.
senses.example: The meeting seemed to drag on for hours, with nobody willing to make a decision.

core.definition: To continue for a much longer time than expected, often in a boring or tiring way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'on,' the final word. In fast speech, the g of 'drag' links into the vowel of 'on,' so it sounds like 'dra-GON.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something tedious or too slow, so it usually sounds like a complaint.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'drag on' in everyday talk about meetings, lectures, movies, or long illnesses, as in 'The meeting dragged on for three hours.' A typical reply is 'Yeah, it felt endless.' It is informal and fine for conversation, but avoid it in formal reports.

distinctions.note: Drag out is transitive and means to deliberately lengthen something, as in 'drag out the process,' while drag on is intransitive and describes something that continues too long.
Go on is neutral and simply means continue, while drag on adds a sense that the duration is tiring or dull.

examples.everyday: The movie dragged on for almost three hours, and I kept checking my phone.
examples.professional: The planning meeting dragged on because nobody had read the agenda, so let's keep the next one to thirty minutes.
examples.analytical: The debate dragged on for decades, as each side repeated arguments that neither had reason to abandon.

nuance.analogy: A boring meeting that drags on is like a slow elevator that stops at every floor: each minute feels longer than the last.
common_mistakes: Placing the object between 'drag' and 'on' incorrectly, as in 'drag it on,' which is not used with this meaning.
Using 'drag on' in formal writing, where 'continue for too long' or 'extend' is more appropriate.

conversation.text: The meeting dragged on for three hours.
This lawsuit has been dragging on for years.

senses.definition: To a drastic degree.
senses.example: drastically reduced prices

senses.definition: In a drastic manner.
senses.example: Lisa always wore shorts and a T-shirt, which clashed drastically with her brother's thick winter coat.

core.definition: To a very large, severe or sudden degree, changing something a great deal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DRAS. The middle syllable is short, and the final -ly is a weak 'lee', not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it often describes severe or harsh changes, such as cuts or reductions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use drastically with change, cut, reduce or increase, especially for big or sudden shifts in prices, plans or budgets. It can sound alarming, so use it when the change is truly severe. For a milder change, say significantly or a lot.

distinctions.note: Dramatically emphasizes that a change is striking or visible, while drastically emphasizes severity or harshness.
Significantly is more neutral and often used in statistics; drastically implies a stronger, more sudden or severe change.

examples.everyday: Gas prices have changed drastically since last summer, so I'm driving less.
examples.professional: Our conversion rate dropped drastically after the pricing change, so we need to roll it back this week.
examples.analytical: The interpretation shifts drastically depending on which baseline assumptions one adopts, which weakens the argument.

nuance.analogy: Drastically is like a car brake pressed all the way down: the change is sudden and strong.
nuance.etymology: From drastic, from Greek drastikos 'effective, forceful', from dran 'to do, act'.
common_mistakes: Confusing drastically with dramatically when you mean a noticeable but not severe change.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as dra-STIK-lee.

senses.definition: An open-topped box that can be slid in and out of the cabinet that contains it, used for storing clothing or other articles.
senses.example: She kept her winter sweaters in the bottom drawer of the dresser near the window.

senses.definition: A side panel containing supplementary content.
senses.example: Open the drawer on the right side of the screen to see additional settings and tools.

senses.definition: Attributive form of drawers.
senses.example: The drawer space in our kitchen is too small for all the silverware we own.

senses.definition: Agent noun of draw; one who draws.
senses.example: The drawer of the winning ticket was announced at noon in the town square.

senses.definition: An artist who primarily makes drawings.
senses.example: The local drawer sold pencil sketches of the harbor at the summer art festival.

senses.definition: One who writes a bank draft, check/check, or promissory note.
senses.example: The drawer wrote a check on an account that had insufficient funds to cover it.

senses.definition: A barman; a person who draws the beer from the taps.
senses.example: The drawer poured two pints of ale before the crowd got restless at the pub.

senses.definition: Someone who taps palm sap for making toddy.
senses.example: Before dawn, the drawer climbed the palm tree to collect sap for toddy.
