Using evermore in casual speech where forever sounds more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Psalms, the phrase from this time forth and for evermore expresses God's enduring care and the believer's praise that continues into the future. The Hebrew phrase is ad olam (עַד עוֹלָם), meaning until the age, forever. Psalm 113:2 praises the name of the LORD from this time forth and for evermore; Psalm 121:8 describes the LORD keeping the going out and the coming in from this time forth and for evermore; Psalm 131:3 calls Israel to hope in the LORD from this time forth and for evermore.

evermore.etymology: From Middle English *evermore* (written as two words before 14th century), equivalent to *ever* + *more*.

senses.definition: To make a hole in (something); to hollow.
To remove part of (something) by scooping or digging it out.
senses.example: The archaeologists spent three summers carefully excavating the ash layers beneath the temple.

senses.definition: To uncover (something) by digging.
Any member of a major grouping of unicellular eukaryotes, of the clade Excavata.
senses.example: Many excavates are free-living flagellates found in anoxic freshwater and marine sediments.

senses.definition: (rare) Made hollow.
senses.example: Its excavate core made the old tree trunk light enough to float across the pond.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To dig out earth or material to uncover something, such as ruins or buried objects, or to make a hole by digging.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, EK. The middle syllable is reduced to 'uh', and the ending rhymes with 'rate'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a careful or systematic digging process, often in archaeology or construction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use excavate in archaeology, construction, and mining. In everyday talk they say 'dig' or 'dig up' instead. A news report might say 'archaeologists excavated the site,' while a contractor might say 'we dug out the foundation.'

distinctions.note: Dig is everyday and general; excavate suggests a more careful, systematic removal of material.
Unearth focuses on discovering something hidden; excavate focuses on the digging process.

examples.everyday: The city crew had to excavate part of the street to fix the water pipe.
examples.professional: The contractor will excavate the basement before we pour the new concrete slab.
examples.analytical: Scholars who excavate the ancient city must interpret both the physical layers and the texts found within them.

nuance.analogy: To excavate is like peeling back the layers of an onion carefully, one at a time, to reach what lies inside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excavare, 'to hollow out', from ex- 'out' plus cavare 'to hollow'.
common_mistakes: Using excavate for casual digging in a garden; 'dig' is more natural.
Confusing the verb with the noun excavation, which is the process or the site.

excavate.etymology: from Latin *excavātus* (“hollowed out”), perfect passive participle of *excavō* (“to hollow out”) (see *-ate* and *-ate*), from *ex* (“out”) + *cavō* (“to hollow out, pierce”), from *cavus* (“cave, hole”) + *-ō*.

senses.definition: To be larger, greater than (something).
senses.example: The company's 2005 revenue exceeds that of 2004.

senses.definition: To be better than (something).
senses.example: The quality of her essay has exceeded my expectations.

senses.definition: To go beyond (some limit); to surpass; to be longer than.
senses.example: Your password cannot exceed eight characters.

senses.definition: To predominate.
senses.example: In this neighborhood, renters exceed homeowners, shaping what local issues get attention.

core.definition: To be greater than a limit or amount, or to go beyond what is allowed, expected, or required.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, so the vowel in 'seed' is long and clear. Non-native speakers often shorten it or stress the first syllable, so keep the full long vowel and avoid a soft 'ex' start.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a fact about amounts or limits and carries no praise or blame by itself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exceed for numbers, budgets, speed limits, and expectations, as in 'The bill exceeded my budget.' In casual speech people often say 'go over' instead. In business writing, exceed is very common, and 'exceed expectations' is a standard phrase in performance reviews.

distinctions.note: Surpass usually means doing something better than others, while exceed is about going beyond a number, limit, or expectation.
Pass means to go by or move ahead of something, while exceed implies going past a fixed boundary or quantity.

examples.everyday: Hey, the pizza order came to more than twenty dollars, which exceeded what I planned to spend.
examples.professional: Our team's sales in the third quarter exceeded the target by twelve percent.
examples.analytical: Such a claim exceeds what the evidence can support, since the sample is too small to justify a general conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like water rising over the top of a glass, the amount goes past the edge.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excedere, 'to go out or beyond,' from ex- 'out' and cedere 'to go.'
common_mistakes: Using 'exceed' with a preposition like 'to' or 'from' (say 'exceeded the limit,' not 'exceeded to the limit').
Mixing up the noun 'excess' (stress on the first syllable) with the verb 'exceed' (stress on the second).

exceed.etymology: From Middle English *exceden*, from Old French *exceder*, from Latin *excēdō* (“to go beyond”), from *ex-* (“out, forth”) with *cēdō* (“to go”); see *cede* and compare *accede* etc.

senses.definition: Having excelled, having surpassed.
senses.example: Excellent at chess, she had already surpassed her coach by the end of the season.

senses.definition: Of higher or the highest quality; splendid.
senses.example: We had an excellent dinner at the little Italian place downtown last night.

senses.definition: Exceptionally good of its kind.
senses.example: Bill and Ted had an excellent adventure last week in preparation for their history exam.

senses.definition: Superior in kind or degree, irrespective of moral quality.
senses.example: The lion is an excellent hunter, though its skill says nothing about its character.

core.definition: Extremely good, of very high quality, so that it deserves praise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EK, and the middle syllables reduce to a quick uh. The final -ent is weak, so the word sounds like EK-suh-lent, not ex-SEL-ent.

nuance.connotation: Positive and enthusiastic. It is common in praise, though it can sound a bit formal in casual replies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say excellent casually as a warm reply to good news or an offer, such as 'Excellent, see you Tuesday.' That's excellent! is friendly and natural. In emails and customer service, it is also very common for praising work. In casual talk, great or sounds good is more typical, but excellent is always acceptable.

distinctions.note: Great is broader and more everyday, while excellent implies a higher standard of quality.
Good is a general positive word, while excellent suggests clearly superior quality.
Superb is more emphatic and somewhat more formal than excellent.

examples.everyday: Excellent! Let's grab a table by the window before the line gets long.
examples.professional: Excellent work on the dashboard; the client loved the chart and asked for the same layout next quarter.
examples.analytical: An excellent argument must do more than sound convincing; it must withstand the strongest objections.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-tuned instrument that plays every note clearly.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excellens, present participle of excellere, to rise above, excel.
common_mistakes: Using excellent as a verb, as in 'I excellent at math'; say 'I excel at math' or 'I'm excellent at math'.
Using excellent with a noun ending that sounds awkward, such as 'an excellently idea'; the adjective is the right form.

excellent.etymology: From Middle English *excellent*, from Old French *excellent*, from Latin *excellēns* (“elevated, exalted”), present participle of *excellō* (“elevate, exult”), equivalent to *excel* + *ent*.

senses.definition: Liable or subject to excise.
senses.example: Tobacco is an excisable commodity.

senses.definition: Able to be excised.

core.definition: Able to be cut out or removed, or liable to an excise tax on goods.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SY, the second syllable. The s in excise is pronounced like z, and the -able ending is reduced to 'uh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a technical or legal status.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, excisable appears mainly in medical writing, where it describes a lesion that can be cut out, and in tax law, where it describes goods subject to federal or state excise taxes. In everyday talk people say 'removable' or 'taxable' instead.

distinctions.note: Removable is a general term; excisable implies cutting something out, especially surgically or from a text.
Taxable covers any income or property; excisable refers specifically to goods subject to an excise tax.

examples.everyday: The bartender said imported spirits are excisable, which is why the price is higher.
examples.professional: Our finance team confirmed that the vaping products are excisable, so they must be reported on a separate line.
examples.analytical: Whether a tumor is excisable depends on its location and its relation to vital structures, not only on its size.

nuance.analogy: Like a bad spot on an apple that you can cut away cleanly, an excisable item is one that can be taken out.
nuance.etymology: From excise (verb), from Latin excidere, to cut out, with the suffix -able meaning capable of being.
common_mistakes: Confusing excisable (adjective) with excise (verb or noun) in tax and medical contexts.
Pronouncing the s in excise as a hard s instead of a z sound.

senses.definition: To inflict intense pain or mental distress on (someone); to torture.

core.definition: To cause someone intense physical or mental pain, so severe that it feels like torture.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SKROO, the second syllable. The 'ci' is pronounced 'sh,' and the final '-ate' is a long 'ayt,' not 'ut.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes very strong pain or suffering, so it should be used for serious situations, not mild annoyances.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, the verb 'excruciate' is less common than its adjective 'excruciating,' which people use constantly for everyday hyperbole, as in 'excruciating wait.' Using the verb itself sounds formal or literary, so in conversation Americans often say 'it was torture' or 'it killed me.' Reserve the verb for serious writing or a deliberately dramatic tone.

distinctions.note: Torture implies deliberate, systematic cruelty by one person toward another. Excruciate describes the effect of intense pain, whether or not anyone intended it.
Agonize can mean suffering or worrying over a decision. Excruciate is more intense and usually describes physical or overwhelming pain.
Torment suggests prolonged, persistent suffering or harassment. Excruciate focuses on the sharp, intense quality of the pain.

examples.everyday: Stepping on a Lego barefoot would excruciate anyone, so I always check the floor before I walk in my kids' room.
examples.professional: Long, unclear status meetings can excruciate the team, so keep your updates short and specific.
examples.analytical: Dostoevsky's question asks whether a world that could excruciate a child can be justified, a question that still troubles believers.

nuance.analogy: Like a splinter pressed deeper with every movement: the pain grows sharper the more it is touched.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excruciare, 'to torment greatly,' from ex- ('out' or 'thoroughly') and cruciare ('to torture'), related to crux ('cross').
common_mistakes: Using 'excruciate' for mild discomfort; the word means severe pain, so save it for serious situations.
Pronouncing 'ci' as 'see' instead of 'sh,' or ending the word as 'excruciate' with a short vowel instead of 'ayt.'
Confusing the verb 'excruciate' with the more common adjective 'excruciating' in everyday speech.

excruciate.etymology: From Latin *excruciatus*, past participle of *excrucio*, from *ex* + *crucio*, from the base of *crux* (“cross”).

senses.definition: Capable of being executed.
senses.example: The installer produces an executable file that runs on any Windows laptop without extra setup.

senses.definition: A file that can be run directly by a computer's hardware or a p-code interpreter with no further processing.
senses.example: The program as written by the programmer is generally processed into an executable that can be run.

core.definition: Able to be carried out or run; in computing, a program file that a computer can run directly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'EK'. The 'ex' is pronounced 'ek' here, and the ending '-able' is a weak syllable, 'uh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes something that can be carried out or run.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday talk Americans usually say 'feasible' or 'doable' for a plan. In software, 'executable' is standard, and users call the file an 'app' on phones or an '.exe' on Windows. Use it in technical contexts for running code.

distinctions.note: Feasible means practical or achievable; executable is more formal and can mean a plan that can be carried out or a program that can run.
Runnable is informal engineering shorthand for code or scripts that can start; executable is the standard term for a file a system can run.

examples.everyday: Your road trip idea sounds fun, but is it really executable with only two weekends?
examples.professional: Once the build passes, the executable goes to staging, where QA will smoke test it.
examples.analytical: A plan that is logically consistent is not thereby executable; the real question is whether its steps survive contact with the world.

nuance.analogy: An executable file is like a sealed recipe the computer can cook directly, without a translator reading it first.
nuance.etymology: From execute, from Latin exsequi 'to follow out, carry through', plus the suffix '-able'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable with a long 'ee' vowel; keep 'EK-sih'.
Confusing executable with 'executive', which is a manager or a branch of government.

senses.definition: Something fit to be imitated; an ideal, a worthy model or role model: a desirable example.
senses.example: Michelangelo's "David" is an exemplar of Renaissance sculpture.

senses.definition: Something typical or representative; an example that typifies its class.
senses.example: Her quiet courage made her an exemplar for every nurse on the ward.

senses.definition: A pattern after which others should be made; an archetype.
senses.example: The cathedral became the exemplar for Gothic churches built across northern Europe.

senses.definition: A well-known use of a scientific theory.
senses.example: The double-helix model is an exemplar of how a theory can reshape an entire field.

senses.definition: A manuscript used by a scribe to make a handwritten copy; the original document to be reproduced in a copy machine.
senses.example: The monk copied the psalter from an exemplar that had been kept in the abbey library.

senses.definition: A copy of a book or piece of writing.
senses.example: Our library owns an exemplar of the first edition, though its pages are badly foxed.

core.definition: A person, thing or model that is worth imitating, or a typical example of its kind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, zem. The final syllable is a reduced 'er' sound, not a clear 'ar' as in 'car'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a model worth following.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exemplar in writing about leadership, careers, history and art. In everyday speech people say role model, example or best. It sounds elevated, so use it when you want to praise someone's standard.

distinctions.note: An example can be any instance, while an exemplar is a particularly good or typical model to follow.
Role model is everyday and personal, while exemplar is more formal and can refer to a type or pattern as well as a person.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was an exemplar of patience, and everyone in the family knows it.
examples.professional: Her project is the exemplar we'll use when we write the team's onboarding guide.
examples.analytical: The saint is an exemplar of humility, though the text complicates whether imitation is possible.

nuance.analogy: Like a standard meter bar kept in a vault, against which every other ruler is measured.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exemplar, copy or model, from eximere, to take out or copy.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'zam' instead of 'zem'.
Using exemplar for an ordinary example in casual speech; it sounds too formal.

exemplar.etymology: From Middle English *exempler*, from Middle French *exemplair*, and its source, Latin *exemplar*, from Latin *exemplum* (“example”).

senses.definition: That exists, or has existence, especially that exists now.

core.definition: Currently in place, in use, or already present, especially as opposed to planned, proposed, or future things.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZIS, with a short i. The x is pronounced as g-z, and the ending -ing is a short ing, not eeng.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word that signals what is already in place.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use existing constantly in business and daily life, as in existing customers or existing policy. It sounds natural before a noun. For right now, Americans often say current instead, which focuses on the present moment rather than on what has already been established.

distinctions.note: Current focuses on the present time; existing focuses on what is already in place, even if the time is not specified.
Existent is more formal and philosophical, often meaning simply having reality; existing is the everyday word for what is already in place.

examples.everyday: Can I use my existing coupon on this, or do I need to get a new one?
examples.professional: We'll build the new dashboard on top of the existing data warehouse rather than replacing it.
examples.analytical: Any theory of causation must account for existing regularities without assuming that they will continue indefinitely.

nuance.analogy: Like a house already built: you can renovate it, but you start from the walls that are standing.
nuance.etymology: Present participle of exist, from Latin existere.
common_mistakes: Using existing when you mean current, as in the existing time, which sounds odd; use current time instead.
Pronouncing the ending as eeng instead of a short ing.

senses.definition: One who exploits.
senses.example: The exploiter of the factory's workers was finally arrested by federal investigators.

senses.definition: To make use of (something).
senses.example: The startup hoped to exploit its loyal users' data without reading the privacy terms.

core.definition: A person who takes unfair advantage of others, or who makes profitable use of something, often at others' expense.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPLOY. The final syllable -er is a weak, reduced vowel, so say it as tur. Do not confuse the spelling with 'exploit' as a verb ending in -t.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes someone who takes unfair advantage and is usually a term of criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exploiter mainly in news, politics, labor discussions and academic writing. It is a strong word, so use it to describe real unfairness rather than simply a tough negotiator. In everyday talk, people more often say 'someone who takes advantage of people' or use the verb exploit.

distinctions.note: A profiteer makes money from a crisis or shortage, while an exploiter takes unfair advantage of workers, customers or others in general.
User is a neutral term for someone who uses something, while exploiter is negative and implies unfairness.

examples.everyday: Some landlords in this town are real exploiters, so my roommate and I are looking for a place from a family who treats tenants fairly.
examples.professional: We should not work with vendors who are exploiters of contract workers, even if their prices look better on paper.
examples.analytical: Marx treats the capitalist as the exploiter of labor, but the moral question is whether exploitation can be measured without assuming a theory of value.

nuance.analogy: An exploiter is like a tenant who strips a rented apartment for parts and leaves the building worse than they found it.
nuance.etymology: From exploit, from Old French esploit, achievement, from Latin explicitum, unfolded, plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using exploiter as a verb, as in 'they exploiter the workers'. The verb is exploit.
Using exploiter as a neutral term for anyone who uses something, when it usually carries a strong negative meaning.

senses.definition: The action of expressing thoughts, ideas, feelings, etc.
A particular way of phrasing an idea.
senses.example: Her apology was a clumsy expression of regret that satisfied nobody.

senses.definition: A colloquialism or idiom.
senses.example: The expression "break a leg!" should not be taken literally.

senses.definition: A facial appearance usually associated with an emotion.
senses.example: They stared at the newcomer with a puzzled expression.

senses.definition: An arrangement of symbols denoting values, operations performed on them, and grouping symbols.
senses.example: Simplify the expression by expanding the parentheses before solving for x.

senses.definition: A piece of code in a high-level language that returns a value.
senses.example: The lambda expression returns the squared value of each item in the list.

senses.definition: A specific blend of whisky.
senses.example: The distillery's new expression is smoky, with notes of honey and vanilla.

senses.definition: Emotional involvement or engagement in a text read aloud rendered by the voice of the reciter or the reader.
senses.example: Her expression as she read the poem made the whole room go quiet.

senses.definition: The process of translating a gene into a protein.
senses.example: Hormones can change how strongly a gene's expression produces its protein.

senses.definition: The act of pressing or squeezing out.
senses.example: expression from a gland

senses.definition: The tone of voice or sound in music.
senses.example: The singer's expression in the slow verse was tender and restrained.

core.definition: The act of putting thoughts, feelings, or ideas into words, looks, or actions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on PRESS, and the ending -sion is a single shun sound, not shee-on. Keep the r clear in press and do not say ek-SPRESS-ee-un.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can praise genuine feeling, but a facial expression can also show displeasure, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expression for both the act of expressing and the result, as in freedom of expression or a strange expression on someone's face. In everyday talk people often say show or say rather than express a feeling. The word is most common in formal, written or artistic contexts.

distinctions.note: An expression is what you show or say; an impression is the idea or feeling other people form about you.
Expression is a particular act or look; expressiveness is the general quality of being vivid and expressive.

examples.everyday: Did you catch his expression when they said the bill was late?
examples.professional: Please include a clear expression of the budget constraints in the proposal.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard treats despair as an expression of the self's refusal to become itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a window: it lets the inside of a room show outward.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expressio, from exprimere, to press out.
common_mistakes: Saying make an expression when the verb express is needed: I want to express my thanks, not make an expression of thanks.
Using expression for an everyday idiom in casual talk, where idiom or saying is more natural.

expression.etymology: Middle French *expression*, from Late Latin *expressiō* (“a pressing out”).

senses.definition: Of a person: emaciated, wasted, weakened; of the body or part of it: atrophied, shrunken, withered.
senses.example: After months of illness, the extenuate old man could barely lift the spoon to his mouth.

senses.definition: Of a quality or thing: lessened, weakened.
senses.example: By midterms, his extenuate interest in calculus had dwindled to almost nothing.

senses.definition: Reduced to poverty; impoverished.
senses.example: The extenuate family lost their farm and lived on charity for years.

senses.definition: To make (something) less dense, or thinner; also, to lower the viscosity of (something).
senses.example: The chemist used heat to extenuate the solution, thinning it for the next stage of the experiment.

senses.definition: To make (someone or something) slender or thin; to emaciate, to waste.
senses.example: Years of famine had extenuated the villagers until they were little more than skin and bone.

senses.definition: To underestimate or understate the importance of (something); to underrate.
senses.example: to extenuate his faults to extenuate their crimes

senses.definition: To diminish or seek to diminish the extent or severity of (a crime, guilt, a mistake, or something else negative) by making apologies or excuses; to palliate.
senses.example: to extenuate his faults to extenuate their crimes

senses.definition: To beat or draw (a metal object, etc.) out so as to lessen the thickness.
senses.example: The smith would extenuate the copper sheet with a hammer until it was paper-thin.

senses.definition: To reduce the quality or quantity of (something); to lessen or weaken the force of (something).
senses.example: Her apology did little to extenuate the damage caused by her careless remarks.

senses.definition: To degrade (someone); to detract from (someone's qualities, reputation, etc.); to depreciate, to disparage.
senses.example: Critics often extenuate the novel's achievements by focusing only on its clumsy dialogue.

core.definition: To make a wrongdoing seem less serious by providing circumstances or reasons that partly excuse it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on STEN, and the middle syllable is 'yoo,' not 'yuh-wuht.' The final syllable is 'ayt,' rhyming with 'eight.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly formal. It describes an attempt to reduce blame, so it can imply someone is making excuses.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this verb mainly in formal writing, legal or ethical discussion, or news. In everyday talk they say 'make an excuse for' or 'explain away.' The adjective 'extenuating' is much more common in American English, especially in 'extenuating circumstances.'

distinctions.note: Mitigate is more common in everyday and legal American English and means to make something less severe, while extenuate specifically focuses on excusing a fault.
Excuse is a common everyday word that names a reason given, while extenuate is a formal verb describing the act of reducing blame.

examples.everyday: He tried to extenuate being late by blaming the traffic on the bridge.
examples.professional: The post-mortem report does not extenuate the missed deadlines, but it does explain them.
examples.analytical: Kant argued that no inclination or circumstance can extenuate a violation of the moral law.

nuance.analogy: Extenuate is like putting a soft cushion under a fall: the impact is still there, but it feels less serious.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extenuare, to make thin, from ex- plus tenuis, thin.
common_mistakes: Using 'extenuate' to mean 'extend' or 'stretch out.'
Saying 'ex-TEN-yoo-ate,' with the stress on the wrong syllable.

extenuate.etymology: From Middle English *extenuat* (“ made thin, emaciated”), from Latin *extenuātus* (“diminished, reduced, thinned”), perfect passive participle of *extenuō* (“to diminish, reduce, thin”) (see *-ate*), from *ex-* + *tenuō*, from *tenuis* (“fine, slender,…

senses.definition: (archaic) Extremely wicked.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: Extremely wicked; describing someone who commits monstrous crimes or acts of great evil.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SIN, and the final syllable is a weak 'us'. Americans reduce the middle vowels to a quick schwa, so avoid saying each syllable clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it is a strong, old-fashioned condemnation of wickedness and is nearly always used to describe a person or deed.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, bookish word that you will mostly meet in older novels, historical writing, or formal criticism. Americans would normally say 'evil', 'wicked', or 'monstrous' in everyday speech. Using it in casual conversation would sound pretentious, though it can be a deliberate, witty choice in writing.

distinctions.note: 'Wicked' is common and can be playful in American speech; 'facinorous' is rare, formal, and carries much stronger moral condemnation.
'Nefarious' describes secret or evil plans or schemes, while 'facinorous' focuses on the monstrous character of the crimes themselves.

examples.everyday: My book club argued about whether the king was just misunderstood, but most of us agreed he was facinorous.
examples.professional: In the editorial, the columnist called the company's cover-up a facinorous act that harmed thousands of workers.
examples.analytical: Milton's depiction of Satan rests on the tension between his intellect and a character that the poem presents as facinorous from the start.

nuance.analogy: Like a word carved in stone rather than written in pencil, it is old, heavy, and built for solemn judgment.
nuance.etymology: From Latin facinorosus, 'wicked', from facinus, 'deed' or 'crime'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'facetious', which means joking inappropriately.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'FAS-in-ous'.

facinorous.etymology: Latin *facinorōsus*, from *facinus* (“deed, bad deed”), from *faciō* (“to make, to do”).

senses.definition: State or condition of not meeting a desirable or intended objective, opposite of success.
senses.example: heart failure

senses.definition: Omission to do something, whether or not it was attempted, especially something that ought to have been done.
senses.example: His failure to file the tax form on time cost him a penalty.

senses.definition: An object, person or endeavor in a state of failure, has failed at something or incapable of success.
senses.example: After three years without a single sale, he felt like a failure.

senses.definition: Termination of the ability of an item to perform its required function; breakdown.
senses.example: The failure of the furnace left our house freezing during the January storm.

senses.definition: Bankruptcy.
senses.example: The bank's failure forced the government to seize its assets overnight.

senses.definition: A condition in which a specified organ does not function well enough to support life.
senses.example: heart failure

core.definition: The condition of not achieving a goal or not working as intended; the opposite of success.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ure' ending is a single reduced syllable pronounced 'yer', not 'fail-YOOR'. In American speech the final r is r-colored.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an unsuccessful outcome, though Americans often treat failure as part of learning in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'failure' for projects, machines, relationships and people, and it can sound harsh when applied to a person directly. In casual speech, people say 'it didn't work out' or 'it fell through' to soften it. Business culture in the United States often treats failure as a learning experience, so you may hear phrases like 'fail fast' in meetings.

distinctions.note: An 'error' is a single mistake in a process, while 'failure' describes the overall result not meeting its goal.
'Defeat' implies losing to an opponent in a contest, while 'failure' can occur without any opponent.

examples.everyday: The cake was a complete failure, but at least we had a good laugh about it while eating the pizza.
examples.professional: The failure rate of the new sensor is about two percent, which is above our acceptable threshold for production.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of evil treats moral failure not as a thing but as a privation, a falling away from the good that a creature was made to pursue.

nuance.analogy: Failure is like a missed step on a staircase: it shows you where the ground was not where you expected, and that information is useful.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-Norman 'failure', from 'faillir', from Latin 'fallere', meaning 'to deceive' or 'to disappoint'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'fail-YOOR', which is not standard American speech.
Using 'a failure' for a single small error; 'an error' or 'a mistake' is more precise.

failure.etymology: From Anglo-Norman *failer*, from Old French *faillir* (“to fail”).

senses.definition: Suitable for use only during fair weather.
senses.example: The fair-weather tent is fine for summer camping but leaks in a storm.

senses.definition: Dependable only in the absence of trouble.

core.definition: Dependable only when things are going well; unreliable and absent when support is needed during trouble or hardship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'weth' in 'weather', with a lighter stress on 'fair'. The 'th' is voiced, so the tongue touches the teeth and the voice keeps going; the final syllable is a weak schwa-r.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes people or things that disappear when conditions get difficult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fair-weather' figuratively for friends, fans, or supporters who are loyal only when times are good. It can also be literal, as in 'fair-weather boating gear', but the figurative sense is far more common. The phrase is usually used to criticize, so use it carefully in front of the person you are describing.

distinctions.note: 'Fickle' describes someone who changes feelings or loyalties often, while 'fair-weather' specifically describes someone who disappears in hard times.
'Bandwagon' describes someone who joins a popular cause late, while 'fair-weather' describes someone who leaves when support is needed.

examples.everyday: He was all smiles when we were winning, but he disappeared as soon as we lost, a real fair-weather friend.
examples.professional: We need dependable partners, not fair-weather vendors who vanish when the project hits a rough patch.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's account of friendship distinguishes lasting virtue-based friendship from fair-weather friendship based only on pleasure or advantage.

nuance.analogy: A fair-weather friend is like an umbrella that only shows up when the sun is shining, and is nowhere to be found when the rain starts.
nuance.etymology: From fair (pleasant) plus weather; the figurative sense developed from the idea of conditions that are only suitable in good weather.
common_mistakes: Using 'fair-weather' only for literal weather, when the figurative sense is far more common.
Writing 'fairweather' as one word; the standard form is hyphenated.

senses.definition: Synonym of falling out (“rift following a disagreement or quarrel”).
senses.example: We had a fall out, couldn't come to terms and haven't talked since.

senses.definition: To come out of something by falling.
senses.example: I opened the cupboard and a can fell out onto my foot.

senses.definition: To cease to be on friendly terms.
senses.example: Dave and I fell out after a long argument.

senses.definition: To give way under someone.
senses.example: The board he was walking on fell out.

senses.definition: To cause someone to slip and/or fall down.
senses.example: The ground fell out from under him.

senses.definition: To be enthusiastic about something; to laugh very hard.
senses.example: When the band started, everybody fell out.

senses.definition: To depart.
senses.example: The guests began to fall out of the chapel slowly after the benediction.

senses.definition: To collapse; to pass out from intoxication.
senses.example: He had one too many at the wedding and fell out on the dance floor.

senses.definition: To be shocked by something.
senses.example: I just about fell out when the bill arrived.

senses.definition: To leave one's place in the current formation of ranks in order to take one's place in a new formation.
senses.example: The sergeant told the platoon to fall out for chow and rejoin at noon.

senses.definition: To leave one's current location to report for duty at a new location.
senses.example: The company fell out for an artillery drill.

senses.definition: (dated) To turn out, happen.
senses.example: Well, it all fell out exactly as the old preacher had predicted.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To stop being on friendly terms with someone after a disagreement or argument.

pronunciation.tip: Stress out, which has the diphthong of cow. The t at the end is a clear stop, not a flap, because it is at the end of the word.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a painful break in a relationship, though it can be used lightly about small arguments.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fall out with a person to describe a friendship or family relationship that breaks down after a quarrel: 'He fell out with his brother over money.' It is informal and common in everyday talk. Note that fallout as a noun means the consequences of an event, or radioactive dust, so do not confuse the two. A natural response is 'Oh no, I'm sorry to hear that.'

distinctions.note: Fall out with someone is about a quarrel between friends or family, while fall out of love is about romantic feelings ending.
Break up usually refers to ending a romantic relationship or a group, while fall out describes a friendship or family relationship that becomes hostile.

examples.everyday: My brother and I fell out over money, and we barely talk now.
examples.professional: The two cofounders fell out over equity, and the startup eventually split.
examples.analytical: Historians note how theological friends fell out over the question of grace and works, leaving lasting divisions in the community.

nuance.analogy: Like two boats that drift apart after the rope between them snaps.
nuance.etymology: Fall comes from Old English feallan; out comes from Old English ut.
common_mistakes: Using fall out to with a person; the standard phrase is fall out with.
Confusing the phrasal verb fall out with the noun fallout, which means consequences or radioactive dust.

senses.definition: To indulge in fantasy; to imagine things only possible in fantasy.
senses.example: I fantasized about my ideal date.

senses.definition: To portray in the mind, using fantasy.
senses.example: At night she would fantasize about moving to Paris and opening a bakery.

core.definition: To imagine something in vivid detail, often something unlikely or impossible, usually for pleasure or escape.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending -ize is pronounced like eyes, so it rhymes with the word size, not with fizz.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to lightly playful. It can describe harmless daydreaming, but it can also suggest unrealistic wishing, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fantasize in casual talk about dreams like buying a house or quitting a job. It is usually followed by about, as in fantasize about winning the lottery, not by of. In a formal or academic context, it can describe imagined alternatives or idealized pasts.

distinctions.note: Daydream is usually brief and spontaneous, while fantasize suggests a more elaborate and deliberate imagined scenario.
Imagine is the general word for forming a mental picture; fantasize adds the sense of indulging in a pleasant or unrealistic scenario.

examples.everyday: I spend every long meeting fantasizing about a beach in Hawaii.
examples.professional: Don't fantasize about a perfect launch; let's plan for the bugs we already know about.
examples.analytical: Nostalgic readers often fantasize about a past free of constraints, forgetting the institutions that made it livable.

nuance.analogy: Directing a private movie in your head, where you control every scene.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the noun fantasy plus the verb-forming suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
Writing fantasize of instead of fantasize about, which is the usual preposition.

senses.definition: In a fastidious manner.

core.definition: In a very careful, precise way, paying close attention to small details and cleanliness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on TID, the same as fastidious. Keep the final -ly as a clear lee, and do not add an extra syllable between dee and us.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing careful work; can imply excessive care when describing habits.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this adverb in speech; they would more likely say 'very carefully' or 'really particular about.' You will see it in writing, reviews, and descriptions of craftsmanship or meticulous habits.

distinctions.note: Carefully is common and neutral; fastidiously suggests a higher level of fussy precision.
Meticulously emphasizes thoroughness and accuracy; fastidiously adds a sense of particular concern for cleanliness and order.

examples.everyday: She keeps her kitchen fastidiously clean, even on a Tuesday night.
examples.professional: The documentation was fastidiously reviewed before we handed it off to the client.
examples.analytical: The author fastidiously distinguishes between the two senses of 'grace' throughout the chapter.

nuance.analogy: Like a jeweler who polishes each facet before the stone goes into the setting.
nuance.etymology: From fastidious plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable, FAS-tid-ee-us-lee.
Using it in casual speech where very carefully would sound more natural.

senses.definition: A feast, or an occasion on which people or animals feast.
senses.example: The village's feasting went on late into the night after the harvest was gathered.

core.definition: A large, festive meal or celebration with plenty of food and drink, often shared with family or friends.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FEE. The vowel is a long ee, so say FEES-ting, not FIS-ting. The final -ing is a short, reduced syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests generosity, celebration, and abundance, though it can sound excessive if overindulgence is the focus.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use feasting in holiday talk, such as a Thanksgiving feasting, or in writing about celebrations. In everyday speech people usually say 'a big meal,' 'a feast,' or 'a spread.' Feasting as a noun is fairly literary, so in casual talk a simple phrase like 'we had a big dinner' is often better.

distinctions.note: Feast is the more common noun for a big meal, while feasting refers more to the act or occasion of eating and celebrating together.
A banquet is a formal, planned dinner for many guests, while feasting can be casual or informal among family.

examples.everyday: After the game we had a big feasting at my cousin's house, with pizza, ribs, and way too much cake.
examples.professional: The team's offsite ended with a long dinner of feasting and toasts, which did more for morale than any slide deck.
examples.analytical: In the parable the father's feasting marks the restoration of the lost son, showing that joy is the proper response to return.

nuance.analogy: Like a long table at a family reunion, where every dish is passed around and nobody leaves hungry.
nuance.etymology: From feast (Old French feste, from Latin festum 'festival') with the -ing noun suffix.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel short, as in FIS-ting; it has a long ee sound.
Using feasting as a countable noun in the plural without context; it is usually uncountable or used with a determiner.
nuance.biblical_note: Feasting appears throughout Scripture as a sign of joy, covenant, and celebration. Luke 15:23 describes the father in the parable of the prodigal son calling for a feast, and Proverbs 15:15 says a cheerful heart has a continual feast. Revelation 19:9 speaks of the marriage supper of the Lamb as a blessed feast. The Hebrew mishteh (feast, drinking) and the Greek heorte (festival) lie behind many such passages.

senses.definition: The tendency of a design project or product cycle to accumulate more and more features or details, rather than to be completed and released at a more basic level.
senses.example: Our sales division promised our client a feature in our software that is currently not feasible for us to implement, which will certainly lead to feature creep.

core.definition: The gradual addition of extra features to a product or project, making it larger, later, and more complicated than planned.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, FEE-cher, with a lighter stress on 'creep.' The word 'creep' is short and clear, so say it with a firm 'kreep' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a problem that delays projects and raises costs.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers and product managers in the United States use this term when a project keeps adding requests, often during development. It is usually said with frustration, as in 'we have feature creep again.' 'Scope creep' is the broader term for any project's growing goals, while feature creep focuses on product features.

distinctions.note: Scope creep covers any growth in a project's goals, while feature creep refers specifically to adding product features.
Gold plating is adding unnecessary polish or quality, while feature creep is adding more functions or options.

examples.everyday: My kitchen remodel turned into feature creep: first a dishwasher, then a whole new island.
examples.professional: We need to freeze the roadmap now to stop feature creep before the launch.
examples.analytical: Feature creep illustrates how incremental, locally reasonable decisions can produce an unmanageable whole.

nuance.analogy: Like a snowball rolling downhill, growing a little with every turn until it is too big to control.
nuance.etymology: 'Feature' is from Old French 'faiture'; 'creep' is from Old English 'crēopan,' to move slowly on the body.
common_mistakes: Using the noun 'feature creeping' as a noun; 'feature creep' is the noun, and 'feature-creep' is an informal verb.
Using it for bugs or errors; it refers only to adding features.

senses.definition: Pertaining to fideism.

core.definition: Relating to fideism, the view that religious faith is independent of reason, or to views and claims that express it.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the IS syllable, not on the first syllable. Keep the first syllable as 'fy' and make the unstressed syllables short and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic description, but often critical in debate, where it suggests that a claim is protected from argument.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective in academic writing and philosophical or theological debate, as in 'a fideistic approach' or 'fideistic claims'. Describing a view as fideistic often signals that it resists rational scrutiny. In conversation at church, say something plainer, such as 'faith without proof'.

distinctions.note: 'Fideist' names a person, while 'fideistic' is the adjective describing a view, claim or approach.
'Faithful' is an everyday word for loyal or trusting, while 'fideistic' names a specific philosophical position about reason.

examples.everyday: Their argument sounded fideistic to me, like they just wanted to end the discussion.
examples.professional: The paper's fideistic conclusion would be hard to defend in a peer-reviewed journal.
examples.analytical: A fideistic account of faith may shield religious belief from criticism, but it also places faith beyond the reach of rational examination.

nuance.analogy: A fideistic claim is like a locked door: argument cannot open it, only trust can.
nuance.etymology: From fideism, formed with the adjective suffix -istic, ultimately from Latin fides, faith.
common_mistakes: Using 'fideistic' to mean 'faithful' in everyday conversation
Stressing the first syllable, as in FY-deh-iss-tik
Using it as a noun instead of as an adjective

senses.definition: An extreme form of constructivism, according to which a mathematical object does not exist unless it can be constructed from natural numbers in a finite number of steps.

core.definition: An extreme form of constructivism holding that a mathematical object exists only if it can be built from natural numbers in finitely many steps.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The ending is /ɪzəm/ with a short i and a weak final syllable, so it sounds like 'tiz-um', not 'tiz-ism'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It names a position in the philosophy of mathematics without any emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'finitism' almost only in academic discussions of logic, philosophy of mathematics and foundations of mathematics. It is closely associated with David Hilbert's program and related debates. In everyday conversation, most people would not recognize it, so explain it briefly if you use it outside a specialist setting.

distinctions.note: Constructivism is the broader view that mathematical objects must be constructed, while finitism is an extreme version that limits construction to finitely many steps from natural numbers.
Intuitionism rejects some classical proofs but still accepts certain infinite processes, while finitism rejects actual infinite collections altogether.

examples.everyday: My logic professor kept talking about finitism, and I still don't quite get what it means.
examples.professional: Our proof avoids infinite sets, so the argument stays within the spirit of finitism.
examples.analytical: Finitism restricts mathematical existence to what can be constructed from the natural numbers in finitely many steps, which rules out actual infinities.

nuance.analogy: Like a builder who will only use bricks that can be carried by hand, refusing any structure that needs a crane the size of the sky.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'finite' and the suffix '-ism', meaning a doctrine or position.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'finitism' with 'finitude', which is a general word for limitedness, not a philosophy of mathematics.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'fi-NYE-tizm'.
Using 'finitism' as a synonym for any cautious view of numbers, when it names a specific extreme position.

senses.definition: A proponent of finitism.
Of or relating to finitism.
senses.example: Primitive recursive arithmetic, or PRA, is a quantifier-free formalization of the natural numbers. It was first proposed by Skolem as a formalization of his finitist conception of the foundations of arithmetic, and it is widely agreed that all reasoning of PRA is finitist. Many also believe that all of finitism is captured by PRA, but others believe finitism can be extended to forms of recursion beyond primitive recursion, up to ε0, which is the proof-theoretic ordinal of Peano arithmetic. PRA's proof theoretic ordinal is ω, where ω is the smallest transfinite ordinal. PRA is sometimes called Skolem arithmetic.

core.definition: A person who holds that mathematics should use only finite objects and methods, rejecting completed infinite sets.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, FY, and the middle vowels are short and reduced, so the word has three clear beats: FY-nih-tist. Non-native speakers often stress the -ist ending or pronounce the middle vowel as a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a philosophical position without praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: You will hear this word mainly in philosophy of mathematics, logic and university seminars, especially when discussing David Hilbert's program. Americans rarely use it in casual talk, so it is safe to reserve it for academic settings. A finitist is the person, finitism is the position, and the adjective is finitist or finitary.

distinctions.note: Both reject some classical reasoning, but an intuitionist accepts potentially infinite processes, while a strict finitist accepts only finite objects and methods.
Constructivism is a broader view that requires existence proofs to build the object; finitism is narrower and limited to finite objects.

examples.professional: As a finitist, she insisted that every step of the proof rest on concrete, checkable constructions rather than on infinite collections.
examples.analytical: The finitist denies that the completed totality of natural numbers exists, so Hilbert's program aimed to secure consistency using only finitary reasoning.

nuance.analogy: A finitist is like a builder who will only lay bricks they can count and touch, refusing to promise a wall whose full size they have never seen.
nuance.etymology: From finite (Latin finitus, bounded or limited) plus the suffix -ist, a person who holds a view.
common_mistakes: Using finitist as an everyday word for someone who is limited or cautious; in ordinary speech say cautious or narrow-minded.
Confusing finitist (a person) with finitism (the position) or finite (the adjective).

senses.definition: Characterized by sudden bursts of activity with periods of inactivity in between; intermittent, irregular, unsteady.
senses.example: His breathing was fitful.

core.definition: Happening in sudden bursts with pauses in between, so irregular and unsteady.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable is a weak schwa followed by l, so it sounds like 'fuhl' with a light vowel. Do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests restlessness, instability or lack of steady effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fitful in writing and in descriptions of sleep, weather or effort, as in 'a fitful sleep' or 'fitful progress'. It is less common in casual speech, where people would say 'on and off' or 'restless'. It is a good word for describing someone who does not sleep well.

distinctions.note: Intermittent is more technical and emphasizes stopping and starting, while fitful adds a sense of restlessness or unevenness.
Erratic suggests unpredictable behavior, while fitful suggests bursts of activity with pauses between.

examples.everyday: I had a fitful night because the baby kept waking up.
examples.professional: Our project made fitful progress last quarter, with long pauses between sprints.
examples.analytical: The author describes the nation's reform as a fitful movement, advancing in brief bursts and then retreating.

nuance.analogy: Fitful work is like a car that starts and stalls, moving forward in jerks rather than in a smooth line.
common_mistakes: Using fitful to mean 'fit' or 'healthy'.
Confusing fitful with fitting, which refers to clothes or a suitable match.

senses.definition: A tool used for threshing, consisting of a long handle (handstock) with a shorter stick (swipple or swingle) attached with a short piece of chain, thong or similar material.
senses.example: The farmer's grandfather still kept an old wooden flail hanging in the barn.

senses.definition: A weapon which has the (usually spherical) striking part attached to the handle with a flexible joint such as a chain.
senses.example: The medieval knight swung a spiked flail, its heavy iron ball whirling on a chain.

senses.definition: Part of a rotating device, often used for cutting vegetation.
senses.example: The mower's flail cut through the tall weeds along the ditch in seconds.

senses.definition: To beat using a flail or similar implement.
senses.example: The trainer flailed a leather strap against the rug to beat out the dust.

senses.definition: To wave or swing vigorously.
senses.example: The toddler flailed her arms wildly while the bus pulled away.

senses.definition: To thresh.
senses.example: By dusk the crew had flailed enough oats to fill three burlap sacks.

senses.definition: To move like a flail.
senses.example: He was flailing wildly, but didn't land a blow.

core.definition: To move your arms or legs wildly and without control, especially when you are falling or struggling.

pronunciation.tip: Use one syllable with a long a sound, rhyming with 'sail'. Make the final l clear and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests awkward, uncontrolled motion, often in panic or struggle.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flail' informally to describe a person or animal waving limbs wildly, such as a child in a pool or someone slipping on ice. It can also describe a struggle, as in 'flailing around for a solution'. The noun for the old farm tool is rare in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: 'Flounder' often means to struggle in confusion or failure; 'flail' focuses on wild, physical arm and leg movements.
'Thrash' suggests violent back-and-forth movement; 'flail' suggests uncontrolled waving of limbs.

examples.everyday: The kid started flailing his arms when he slipped on the wet dock.
examples.professional: The team was flailing for a fix after the server crashed during the launch.
examples.analytical: The essay's argument flails between two incompatible premises without resolving either.

nuance.analogy: Like a kite whose string snaps, its tail whipping in every direction.
nuance.etymology: From Old French flael, from Latin flagellum, 'whip.'
common_mistakes: Using 'flail' only for the farm tool; in everyday American speech the verb is far more common.
Confusing it with 'fail'; 'flail' is pronounced with a clear l at the end.

flail.etymology: From Middle English *flayle*, from earlier *fleil*, *fleyl*, *fleȝȝl*, from Old English *fligel*, **flegel* (“flail”), from **flagil*, of uncertain origin.

senses.definition: A state of floating, or being afloat.
The ability (as of a tire or snowshoes) to stay on the surface of soft ground or snow.
A process of separating minerals by agitating a mixture with water and detergents etc; selected substances being carried to the surface in air bubbles.
senses.example: The mining engineers used flotation to separate copper ore from the waste rock.

core.definition: The state or action of floating on a liquid, or the ability to stay on top of soft ground or snow.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the -tay syllable, and the -tion ending is pronounced 'shun,' not 'tee-on.' The first vowel is a long 'oh,' and the last syllable is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; technical in engineering and mining, but everyday in phrases like 'flotation device.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say 'flotation device' for a life jacket or floating cushion on a boat or plane, and the phrase is official safety language. Vehicle tires and snowshoes are described by their flotation on mud or snow. Mining and chemistry use the term for a separation process, while everyday speakers usually say 'float' or 'floating.'

distinctions.note: Buoyancy is the upward physical force that makes an object rise in a fluid, while flotation is the state or ability of staying up.
Float is the everyday verb and noun for staying on water or air, while flotation is more formal and common in technical or official phrases.

examples.everyday: The flight attendant pointed out the flotation device under our seat before takeoff.
examples.professional: The wide flotation tires let the work truck cross the wet field without sinking.
examples.analytical: The concept of flotation in physics explains how a body displaces its own weight in a fluid, a principle Archimedes formalized.

nuance.analogy: Like a cork bobbing in a glass of water, it stays up because the surface supports it.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'float' plus the suffix '-ation,' the noun ending for an action or state.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'FLOH-tay-shun'; the main stress falls on -TAY.
Mixing up 'flotation' with 'floatation'; both spellings appear, but 'flotation' is more common in American technical use.

senses.definition: That flows; flowing, liquid.
senses.example: fluent handwriting

senses.definition: Able to use a language accurately, rapidly, and confidently.
senses.example: She's fluent in French.

senses.definition: Being or relating to a fluent interface.
senses.example: The payment processor offers a fluent API.

core.definition: Able to speak or write a language easily, accurately, and smoothly, without much hesitation or searching for words.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second vowel is a reduced 'uh'. Avoid making the vowel a long 'oo' sound in the second syllable; end with a clear 't'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Calling someone fluent is a compliment about their ability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'fluent in' followed by a language, as in 'He is fluent in French.' Saying 'He speaks fluent French' is also natural and common. The word can describe smooth speech or writing, but you rarely hear it used for physical objects in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Proficient suggests competence and skill, while fluent stresses ease and natural flow.
Bilingual means speaking two languages, but a bilingual person may not be fluent in both.

examples.everyday: My cousin grew up in Mexico and is fluent in Spanish, so she always helps me order at restaurants.
examples.professional: We need a fluent English speaker to run the customer support call for our Brazilian clients.
examples.analytical: A fluent speaker automates many grammatical choices, which makes fluent speech harder to analyze than halting speech.

nuance.analogy: A fluent speaker is like a skilled driver who moves through traffic without thinking about each turn.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fluens, 'flowing', present participle of fluere, 'to flow'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'fluent of French'; the usual preposition is 'in'.
Using 'fluent' to mean 'fluid' for liquids in everyday speech.

fluent.etymology: From Latin *fluens* (“flowing”), present active participle of *fluō* (“to flow”).

senses.definition: Initialism of footnote.
Diminutive of FN-FAL (the NATO standard rifle)
senses.example: He cleaned his FN carefully before the Saturday range qualification at the base.

senses.definition: Diminutive of FN Five-seven (the pistol derivative of the FN-FAL)
senses.example: She kept her FN in a holster on her hip during the training exercise.

senses.definition: Initialism of fibronectin.
senses.example: The lab measured elevated FN in the plasma samples from patients with fibrosis.

senses.definition: Initialism of false negative.
senses.example: The screening test returned too many FN results, so we retested every sample.

senses.definition: Initialism of falling number.
senses.example: The miller tested the wheat, and its FN was low, suggesting sprout damage.

core.definition: Abbreviation for footnote, a note printed at the bottom of a page that cites a source or adds detail to the main text.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters, not a word: 'ef' and 'EN', with the stress on the second letter. Do not say 'fin' or 'fun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a shorthand for a formal writing device.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use FN informally in drafts, notes, and tables to mean footnote, but in published academic or business writing they usually write footnote in full. In casual speech people say footnote, not the letters. In firearms discussions FN refers to the FN Herstal company and its rifles, which is a different meaning.

distinctions.note: Footnote is the full word used in speech and formal writing; FN is an informal abbreviation mainly for drafts, notes, and tables.
An endnote appears at the end of a chapter or document; a footnote appears at the bottom of the page.

examples.everyday: The article is fine, but check the FN at the bottom because the link might be broken.
examples.professional: Please move the methodology details into an FN so the report stays under ten pages.
examples.analytical: The author places the qualifying argument in an FN, which makes the main claim look cleaner than the evidence allows.

nuance.analogy: An FN is like a sticky note on a page that adds detail without changing the main story.
nuance.etymology: Abbreviation of footnote, from foot (bottom of the page) plus note.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing FN as a word like 'fin' or 'fun'; say the letters ef-EN.
Using FN in formal published writing; write footnote in full.
Confusing the document abbreviation with the FN firearms brand in news or technical talk.

senses.definition: One of a pair of lights, mounted at the front of a car, below the headlights, usually white or yellow in color, for increased visibility ahead in foggy driving conditions.
senses.example: When the morning fog rolled in, I switched on my fog lights before pulling onto the highway.

core.definition: A pair of low lights on the front of a car, below the headlights, that give a wide beam for seeing the road in fog.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FOG in this compound noun, with an open vowel like the a in father, so it is not FOHG. Lights ends in an s sound, and the word is plural because cars normally have two.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a safety feature, so the term is practical and positive in context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say fog lights for the pair of lamps on the front bumper, and the term appears in car manuals and everyday talk about driving in bad weather. Some people also say fog lamps, but fog lights is more common in the US. Use low beams with fog lights, since high beams reflect light back from fog and make visibility worse.

distinctions.note: Headlights are the main forward lights for normal driving; fog lights are lower and wider to light the road surface in fog.
High beams send light far ahead but reflect off fog; fog lights are designed to avoid that glare.

examples.everyday: Turn your fog lights on, it's really murky on the highway.
examples.professional: The fleet safety report recommends fog lights on all vans that operate near the coast.
examples.analytical: Fog lights improve visibility by placing a low, wide beam beneath the fog layer, where headlight beams would reflect back toward the driver.

nuance.analogy: Like a flashlight aimed at your feet on a foggy path instead of into the mist, fog lights light what is directly in front of you.
nuance.etymology: Fog comes from Scandinavian sources of uncertain origin; light comes from Old English lēoht.
common_mistakes: Using high beams in fog instead of fog lights or low beams.
Saying fog light in the singular when the car has two lights.

senses.definition: The part of a department store that sells food.
senses.example: Let's meet at the food hall on the third floor for lunch.

core.definition: An indoor space with several food stalls or counters where people buy and eat meals together.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress falls on FOOD, with a lighter stress on hall. Hall is one syllable; many Americans pronounce it with the 'aw' vowel, and others use a merged 'ah' vowel. Don't add an r.

nuance.connotation: Positive and lively. It suggests variety, local vendors, and a social atmosphere.
nuance.usage_note: In American usage a food hall usually means a modern indoor space with many independent vendors, such as those in downtown developments, transit stations, or office buildings. The older department-store sense, a grocery section, is closer to British usage, where Harrods has a famous food hall; Americans say grocery section, gourmet department, or market instead. In a shopping mall, Americans say food court.

distinctions.note: A food court is usually in a shopping mall and has chain restaurants; a food hall often features independent local vendors.
A market sells raw ingredients and produce; a food hall serves prepared meals to eat on site.

collocations: a food hall with local chefs

examples.everyday: Let's meet at the food hall downstairs, there are about a dozen places to choose from.
examples.professional: The developer wants a food hall on the ground floor to bring foot traffic into the office building.
examples.analytical: The food hall reshapes urban space by turning a transit terminal into a place for social gathering.

nuance.analogy: A food hall is like a potluck that the whole city has been invited to: many cooks, one shared table.
nuance.etymology: Compound of food and hall; hall comes from Old English heall, a large room.
common_mistakes: Confusing food hall with food court; in the US, food court means a mall dining area.
Saying food hall for a single restaurant; a food hall usually has several vendors.

senses.definition: Used to express frustration, exasperation, or annoyance.
senses.example: Oh, for crying out loud, get off the computer! You've been on there for ages!

core.definition: An exclamation of frustration or annoyance, used to show that you are fed up with something someone has done or said.

pronunciation.tip: The 'for' is reduced to a weak 'fer,' and the main stress falls on 'cry' in 'crying.' In speech, 'crying out' links smoothly, so it sounds like 'cry-ing-OWT.'

nuance.connotation: Negative but mild. It expresses exasperation without swearing, so it is considered safe in most settings, including with children.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase as a clean, mild way to vent annoyance, often at home or with coworkers they know well. It sounds slightly old-fashioned or playful and often comes at the start of a sentence. A natural reply is to apologize or laugh, such as 'Sorry, I'll fix it now.' It is not used to express serious anger.

distinctions.note: 'For God's sake' is stronger and can be seen as religious swearing, while 'for crying out loud' is a light, clean expression of annoyance.
'Oh, come on' expresses disbelief or mild impatience, while 'for crying out loud' signals more irritation and exasperation.

collocations: for crying out loud, stop it
for crying out loud, just sit down
for crying out loud, I told you already

examples.everyday: Oh, for crying out loud, I left my keys in the car again.
examples.professional: For crying out loud, the dashboard has been showing stale data since Monday; can someone check the pipeline?
examples.analytical: The phrase 'for crying out loud' softens the force of an oath by substituting a wholesome cry, showing how speakers keep emotional intensity while avoiding offense.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee's whistle used in place of a foul word: it signals the same frustration but keeps the game clean.
common_mistakes: Shortening it to 'for crying out' or dropping 'loud,' which sounds incomplete to native speakers.
Using it for serious anger or grief, where it sounds too light.
Pronouncing 'crying' with a long 'i' and no stress shift, so the phrase sounds flat.

senses.definition: Any mathematical rule expressed symbolically.
senses.example: x=−b±b2−4ac2a is a formula for finding the roots of the quadratic equation ax + bx + c = 0.

senses.definition: A plan or method for dealing with a problem or for achieving a result.
senses.example: The company's winning formula includes excellent service and quality products.

senses.definition: A formulation; a prescription; a mixture or solution made in a prescribed manner; the identity and quantities of ingredients of such a mixture.
senses.example: The formula of the rocket fuel has not been revealed.

senses.definition: A fixed phrase or set of words intended to be interpreted non-literally, typically used attitudinally or as part of convention; a formulation.
senses.example: Avoid the typical epistolic formalae, such as "Kind regards".

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) A formal statement of doctrine.
senses.example: The church council adopted a short formula summarizing its doctrine on grace.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of infant formula, drink given to babies to substitute for mother's milk.
senses.example: They tried switching formulas, and it seemed to work: the baby seemed more content while feeding.

senses.definition: A syntactic expression of a proposition, built up from quantifiers, logical connectives, variables, relation and operation symbols, and, depending on the type of logic, possibly other operators such as modal, temporal, deontic or epistemic ones.
senses.example: Every well-formed formula in first-order logic contains only finitely many symbols.

senses.definition: A symbolic expression of the structure of a compound.
senses.example: H2O is the formula for water.

core.definition: A set of symbols or words expressing a mathematical or scientific rule, or a fixed method for achieving a result.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FOR, and the final -la is a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'luh', not 'lah'. The 'mju' is one quick sound, like 'myoo' in a fast pronunciation.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive when it means a reliable method, and neutral or slightly dismissive when it means a predictable approach that ignores the details.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use formula in school, science, math and business for an exact rule or a reliable method, such as the quadratic formula or a winning formula for a campaign. In everyday talk it also means infant formula, which is what most parents mean by formula. Calling something 'just a formula' suggests it is mechanical and may miss the situation.

distinctions.note: An equation states that two expressions are equal and is solved for unknowns; a formula is a general rule that gives a result from given inputs.
A recipe gives steps for cooking or making something; a formula is a symbolic rule or a fixed composition, and it is more often used for chemistry, math or business methods.

examples.everyday: My sister is mixing the baby formula now, so we can head out for dinner after she's done.
examples.professional: Can you add the standard deviation formula to the dashboard so the analysts can check the numbers?
examples.analytical: Many philosophers argue that moral reasoning cannot be reduced to a formula that applies the same way in every case.

nuance.analogy: A formula is like a machine's blueprint: you feed in known parts and get a predictable output.
nuance.etymology: From Latin formula, a diminutive of forma 'shape, form, model'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'lah' rather than a weak 'luh'.
Using 'formula' for a one-off plan; Americans often say 'approach' or 'strategy' for non-rule situations.
Using 'formulas' for the plural in math and science, where 'formulae' is sometimes used in formal writing, though 'formulas' is more common in American usage.

formula.etymology: Latin *formula* (“a small pattern or mold, form, rule, principle, method, formula”), diminutive of *forma* (“a form”).

senses.definition: The quality of being fractious; trouble-making; unruliness.
A peevish or cranky nature.
senses.example: The toddler's fractiousness grew worse every time someone mentioned nap time.

core.definition: The quality of being quarrelsome, irritable, or hard to control; a tendency to cause trouble.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FRAK, and the final syllables -ness are reduced to 'nus.' Keep the 'sh' sound clear and do not stress the ending.

nuance.connotation: Negative; describes a difficult or argumentative disposition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fractiousness in formal commentary, politics, and writing to describe a persistent tendency to quarrel. In everyday talk they usually say 'argumentativeness' or 'being difficult' instead. It is an uncommon word, so use it in writing rather than in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Argumentativeness is more common in everyday American speech and focuses on a habit of arguing.
Belligerence suggests aggressive hostility, while fractiousness is more about quarrelsome irritability.

examples.everyday: Everyone was tired of the fractiousness at the family dinner, so we changed the topic.
examples.professional: The fractiousness within the leadership team slowed our decision-making for two quarters.
examples.analytical: The historian attributes the fractiousness of the colonial assemblies to competing regional interests and personal rivalries.

nuance.analogy: Fractiousness is like a dry, crackling fire that flares up at the smallest spark of disagreement.
nuance.etymology: From fractious plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ness as 'nes' with a full vowel.
Using fractiousness for a single argument; it describes a general quality or tendency.

senses.definition: The condition of being fraudulent; deceitfulness.

core.definition: The quality of being fraudulent; deception used to cheat people or gain something unfairly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FRAW, with the vowel of caught. The d-zh sound is a single smooth sound, and the last syllable is a reduced lunss, not a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it strongly suggests dishonesty and intent to cheat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use fraudulence in conversation; they say fraud for the act or the scheme and fraudulent for the adjective. Fraudulence appears mostly in formal writing, legal analysis, or literary commentary about deception. If you want a natural everyday word, say the fraud or the scam.

distinctions.note: Fraud is the everyday word for a deceptive act or a person who cheats; fraudulence is the abstract quality and is more formal.
Deceit is a broader word for lying or misleading; fraudulence specifically implies cheating for gain or misrepresenting facts.

examples.everyday: When the seller changed the price after I paid, I realized the whole deal had a kind of fraudulence to it.
examples.professional: The audit uncovered signs of fraudulence in the vendor's invoices, so legal has been brought in.
examples.analytical: The essay exposes the fraudulence of a philosophy that promises truth while hiding its own commercial motives.

nuance.analogy: Fraudulence is like a painted wall that looks solid until you push on it and find it is hollow inside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fraudulentia, from fraudulentus, from fraus, fraud or deceit.
common_mistakes: Using fraudulence for simple mistakes; it implies intentional deception.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel, like FRAW-joo-lence, instead of FRAW-juh-lunss.

senses.definition: To become fresh. To become cool.
To be refreshed.
senses.example: After the long hike, we rested by the lake and quickly freshened in the cool evening breeze.

senses.definition: To become cool.
To become not salty, to lose its salinity.
senses.example: The river water begins to freshen once it flows past the estuary and mixes with snowmelt.

senses.definition: To become stronger.
senses.example: wind force three, freshening from the southwest

senses.definition: To begin or resume giving milk, especially after calving; to cause to resume giving milk.
senses.example: The dairy farmer hopes the heifer will freshen next week after calving in the barn.

senses.definition: To make fresh. To make cool.
To refresh; to revive; to renew.
senses.example: A quick nap helped freshen my tired mind before the afternoon meeting began.

senses.definition: To make cool.
To make green (vegetation that has become dry).
