Complex is a general word for something with many parts, while many-sided stresses having several distinct perspectives or aspects.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a many-sided guy: he is a carpenter, a jazz pianist and an excellent cook.
examples.professional: The proposal takes a many-sided view of customer value, including cost, trust, speed and long-term loyalty.
examples.analytical: Any honest account of justice must be many-sided, since no single principle captures every relevant concern.

nuance.analogy: A many-sided person is like a cut diamond: each facet catches the light from a different angle.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from many and side, from Old English sīde.
common_mistakes: Using it for a simple object with no complexity, when the word is about aspects or perspectives.
Saying 'many sided' without the hyphen in formal writing.
Stressing the second syllable of sided, as in sy-DED.

senses.definition: A 42.195-kilometre (26-mile-385-yard) road race.
Any extended or sustained activity.
senses.example: He had a cleaning marathon the night before his girlfriend came over.

senses.definition: To run a marathon.
senses.example: She decided to marathon in Chicago this October after years of training.

senses.definition: To watch or read a large number of instalments of (a film, book, TV series, etc.) in one sitting.
senses.example: We're going to marathon Star Trek next weekend.

core.definition: A long road race of about 42.2 kilometers (26.2 miles). Also any very long, sustained activity or event.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAIR, and make the middle syllable a quick, weak uh. The final syllable has a short AH vowel, so it rhymes with con, not with the vowel of mar.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the race and mildly negative when used for a long, tiring meeting or task.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use marathon for the race and for any long, exhausting activity, such as a marathon meeting or a marathon study session. Calling something a marathon often means it went on too long, so it can be a mild complaint. A natural reply is Yeah, I'm exhausted.

distinctions.note: An ultramarathon is any race longer than a marathon, often measured in miles or hours rather than a fixed distance.
A half marathon is about 21.1 kilometers (13.1 miles), exactly half the distance of a marathon.

examples.everyday: I'm running a marathon in October, so I'm out on the trails every Saturday morning.
examples.professional: The budget review turned into a marathon, so let's schedule a shorter follow-up session next week.
examples.analytical: The argument is a marathon rather than a sprint, since it depends on sustained evidence rather than a single decisive moment.

nuance.analogy: A marathon tests endurance over distance rather than speed in a single moment, like a long savings plan rather than a quick purchase.
nuance.etymology: Named after the Greek town of Marathon, from the legend of a messenger who ran to Athens after the battle there in 490 BC.
common_mistakes: Saying MAR-uh-thon with the vowel of mar; the first vowel is the MAIR sound.
Stressing the last syllable, as in muh-RATH-un, when the main stress falls on the first syllable.

marathon.etymology: From French *marathon*, coined in 1894 by linguist Michel Bréal for the first modern time Olympic Games after Ancient Greek *Μαραθών*, a town northeast of Athens.

senses.definition: A mark on the person of worshippers of the Antichrist; without the mark one cannot buy or sell.

core.definition: In Revelation, a mark that signals loyalty to the Antichrist; people without it cannot buy or sell.

pronunciation.tip: The word of is reduced to uhv and the before a consonant is thuh. Stress beast strongly, and keep the r in mark.

nuance.connotation: Negative and ominous. It refers to a dangerous sign of evil, and it can be used jokingly about technology, but that can offend religious listeners.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mostly in religious conversation, prophecy talk, or pop culture, sometimes as a joke about barcodes, chips, or surveillance. It can sound disrespectful to Christians if used casually, so be careful. A natural reply in a Bible study is to say what the passage says, or to ask what view the speaker holds.

distinctions.note: The number of the beast is the number 666 in Revelation 13:18, while the mark is the sign placed on the body.
The seal of God is the protective sign on God's people in Revelation, which is the opposite of the mark of the beast.
Sign of the beast is a less common variant phrase with the same meaning, but mark of the beast is the standard expression.

collocations: receive the mark of the beast
bear the mark of the beast
the beast out of the sea
warn against the mark of the beast

examples.everyday: My neighbor joked that the new chip in our credit cards was the mark of the beast, but he was only half kidding.
examples.professional: In our seminar on apocalyptic literature, we compared the mark of the beast with the seal of God in Revelation.
examples.analytical: Revelation presents the mark of the beast as a visible sign of allegiance to an earthly power that demands worship and economic loyalty.

nuance.analogy: Like a loyalty tattoo, the mark shows whose side you are on, and it controls who can trade with you.
nuance.etymology: Mark from Old English mearc; beast from Old French beste, from Latin bestia. The phrase comes from Revelation's Greek term charagma, an engraved mark.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing of as 'off'; in normal speech it is reduced to uhv.
Using the phrase lightly in a serious religious conversation without considering how it may sound.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind mark is charagma, an engraved mark, stamp, or inscription, used in Revelation for the sign of allegiance to the beast. Revelation 13:16-17 describes a mark on the right hand or forehead that controls buying and selling. Revelation 14:9-11 warns those who worship the beast and receive its mark that they will face God's judgment. Revelation 13:18 gives the number of the beast, which many interpreters connect with the mark. Scholars disagree about whether the mark is literal or symbolic.

mark-of-the-beast.etymology: From Middle English, 1350–1400; earliest use in Wycliffe's Bible.

senses.definition: Very large in size or extent.
senses.example: Compared to its counterparts from World War II, the Abrams main battle tank is truly massive.

senses.definition: Substantial in mass; bulky, heavy and solid.
senses.example: A massive comet or asteroid appears to have ended the era of the dinosaurs.

senses.definition: To a very great extent; total, utter.
senses.example: The new manager was a massive disappointment to everyone on the team.

senses.definition: Of particularly exceptional quality or value; awesome.
senses.example: Did you see Colbert last night? He was massive!

senses.definition: Affecting a large portion of the body, or severe.
senses.example: a massive heart attack

senses.definition: Having any mass.
senses.example: Some bosons are massive while others are massless.

senses.definition: Homogeneous, having no clear structure or habit.
senses.example: Massive orthoclase is frequently found associated with crystallized quartz.

senses.definition: Not having an obvious crystalline structure.
senses.example: The geologist described the rock as massive, with no visible crystals under the microscope.

senses.definition: A group of people from a locality, or sharing a collective aim, interest, etc.
senses.example: Big up to the Croydon massive!

senses.definition: A homogeneous mass of rock, not layered and without an obvious crystal structure.
senses.example: karst massives in western Georgia

core.definition: Very large in size, amount or extent; huge, heavy and substantial.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The second vowel is a short i as in sit, and the ending is -iv, not -eev.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to strongly positive or negative depending on context; it is dramatic and emphatic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use massive for physically large things and informally as an intensifier, as in a massive headache. It sounds enthusiastic in casual talk. In formal writing, big or substantial is often clearer.

distinctions.note: Huge is the everyday word and less dramatic; massive suggests weight and solidity.
Enormous stresses size beyond what is normal; massive stresses bulk and mass.
Major means important or significant, not physically large; a major decision is not a massive one.

examples.everyday: The kids ate a massive stack of pancakes this morning.
examples.professional: The release caused a massive spike in support tickets, so we need extra staff this week.
examples.analytical: Much of the literature treats the effect as negligible, yet the authors never report the massive uncertainty in their estimates.

nuance.analogy: A massive oak holds its ground because of its bulk, not just its height.
nuance.etymology: From Old French massif, from mass, from Latin massa 'lump'.
common_mistakes: Confusing massive with massage in spelling or sound; the -ive ending is different.
Using massive to mean important; a massive decision sounds odd, so use major or big.

massive.etymology: From Middle English *massif*, from Middle French *massif*, equivalent to *mass* + *ive*.

senses.definition: A maudlin condition.
senses.example: His maudlinism after the third drink embarrassed everyone at the wedding reception.

core.definition: Excessive, tearful sentimentality; a state of foolish or self-indulgent emotion, especially when drinking or speaking.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the second syllable short and reduced so 'maudlin' sounds like two syllables. The ending '-ism' is pronounced '-iz-um' in American English.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes sentiment that seems excessive, self-indulgent or unearned.
nuance.usage_note: Maudlinism is a rare noun, and Americans usually say the adjective maudlin, as in 'He got maudlin after the third drink.' In everyday speech people more often say schmaltz (informal, from Yiddish) for overdone sentiment in a film or speech. Use maudlinism mainly in writing or formal criticism.

distinctions.note: Sentimentality is the general quality of being moved by feeling, and it can be neutral or positive, while maudlinism is always excessive and negative.
Schmaltz is informal American slang for overdone sentiment in art or music, whereas maudlinism is a more formal word for a foolish or tearful state.
Nostalgia is a wistful longing for the past, which can be healthy, while maudlinism is an excessive, self-indulgent emotional display.

examples.professional: The keynote slides were sincere, but the maudlinism of the closing video distracted from the actual results.
examples.analytical: Critics often confuse genuine grief with maudlinism, though the latter depends on an excess of feeling that the work has not earned.

nuance.analogy: Maudlinism is sentiment left out too long, going soggy like bread left in the rain.
nuance.etymology: From maudlin, from Middle English maudelen, from Old French Madeleine, after Mary Magdalene, often painted with swollen, weeping eyes.
common_mistakes: Using maudlinism as a common everyday word; say maudlin as an adjective in most conversation.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'maw-DLIN'; the stress belongs on the first syllable.

senses.definition: The middle layer of the wall of a blood vessel or lymph vessel which is composed of connective and muscular tissue.
A voiced stop consonant.
senses.example: In phonetics class, we learned that b and d are medias, unlike the voiceless p and t.

senses.definition: One of the major veins of the insect wing, between the radius and the cubitus.
senses.example: The entomologist labeled each vein on the dragonfly wing, including the medias between the radius and cubitus.

senses.definition: An ant specialized as a forager in a leaf-cutter ant colony.
senses.example: Each leaf-cutter ant colony depends on medias, specialized foragers that carry fresh leaves back to the nest.

senses.definition: Synonym of cuarto: a half-fanega, a traditional Spanish unit of dry measure equivalent to about 27.8 L.
senses.example: The old recipe called for two medias of barley, a traditional Spanish dry measure.

senses.definition: (“someone who supposedly conveys information from the spirit world”)
senses.example: The grieving widow visited a medium who claimed to be one of the medias for her late husband.

senses.definition: The means and institutions for publishing and broadcasting information.
senses.example: As a result of the rise of, first, television news and entertainment media and, second, web-based media, traditional print-based media has declined in popularity.

senses.definition: The totality of content items (television shows, films, books, photographs, etc.) which are broadcast or published.
senses.example: Fighter pilots are depicted as cool in popular media like Top Gun.

senses.definition: The journalists and other professionals who comprise the mass communication industry.
senses.example: Some celebrities dislike press conferences, where the media bombards them with questions.

senses.definition: Files and data comprising material viewable by humans, but usually not plain text; audiovisual material.
senses.example: Our streaming archive stores millions of medias, from home videos to podcasts and scanned photographs.

senses.definition: Clipping of multimedia.
senses.example: I have media files stored on an external hard drive.

core.definition: The middle layer of a blood or lymph vessel wall, made of smooth muscle and connective tissue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the final s as a z sound. The ending is -iz, not -ia, so it is not like the plural media.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise anatomical term.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English this word is almost never heard. Americans say media for news outlets or for the plural of medium, and they use the Latin phrase tunica media in anatomy. The adjective sense, a clipping of multimedia, is not standard; in professional writing, say multimedia in full.

distinctions.note: Media in American speech means news and communication channels and is a plural of medium; medias is only a technical anatomical term or a rare clipping.
The tunica intima is the innermost layer of a vessel wall, while the medias is the thick muscular middle layer.

examples.everyday: The nurse said the medias, the thick muscular middle layer of an artery, is what keeps it flexible.
examples.professional: The pathology report noted thickening in the medias of the aortic wall, consistent with long-term high blood pressure.
examples.analytical: Histological comparison shows that the medias contains most of the smooth muscle, which explains the vessel's ability to contract.

nuance.analogy: Like the springy middle of a garden hose, between the inner lining and the outer wrap.
nuance.etymology: From Latin media, feminine of medius, middle, as in tunica media, the middle coat.
common_mistakes: Treating medias as the everyday plural of media; in ordinary speech media is the word people use.
Using medias as an adjective; say multimedia instead.

senses.definition: Cooked somewhat lightly, so the meat is no longer red, but is not brown (in the case of beef); cooked to a degree between rare and medium.
senses.example: I'd like my steak medium rare, with a warm red center and a little char.

core.definition: Of meat, especially beef: cooked so the center is warm and red, with a pink, juicy middle.

pronunciation.tip: Say medium with a secondary stress on the first syllable, and stress rare most strongly. The r in both words is strongly pronounced in American English, and medium has no t sound to flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a standard, ordinary way to order steak and carries no judgment about the eater.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say medium rare when ordering steak in restaurants, and the server may ask How would you like it cooked? Common answers are medium rare, medium, or well done. You can simply say medium rare and the kitchen understands. Some people prefer rare or medium well, which are equally normal.

distinctions.note: Rare is cooked less, with a cool red center, while medium rare is warmer with a pink center.
Medium is cooked further, with a warm pink center that is less red than medium rare.

collocations: how do you like it, medium rare?

examples.everyday: I'll have the ribeye, medium rare, please.
examples.professional: Our catering menu lists the steak as cooked medium rare unless the guest asks otherwise.
examples.analytical: In food science, medium rare is defined by an internal temperature of about 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, which keeps the meat tender while killing most surface bacteria.

nuance.analogy: Medium rare is like a warm hug: warm all the way through, but still soft and a little pink in the middle.
nuance.etymology: Medium comes from Latin medius, middle; rare comes from Old English hrere, half-cooked.
common_mistakes: Saying medium-rare as a noun, for example I want a medium rare, which is acceptable in speech but is usually better as I want it medium rare.
Pronouncing rare as ray instead of the r-colored RAIR sound.

conversation.text: How would you like your steak? Medium rare, please.
The chef recommends the lamb medium rare.
I asked for medium rare, but this is almost raw.

senses.definition: Of a program or programming language, not memory-safe.

core.definition: Of a program or programming language, vulnerable to memory errors such as buffer overflows, because it allows direct memory manipulation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on SAFE, with the prefix un- unstressed and reduced to a short uh sound. Keep the first part light, and do not stress the prefix as un-SAFE with a heavy vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it signals risk of crashes and security holes. It is often stated neutrally in technical comparisons, and sometimes as a criticism of older software.
nuance.usage_note: Developers and security researchers use this term most often for C and C++, especially in discussions of vulnerabilities and legacy code. Americans usually say the code or language is memory-unsafe rather than calling a whole company's product that. Use the hyphen before a noun and keep it separate after a verb.

distinctions.note: Memory-safe means the language prevents memory errors, while memory-unsafe means it does not, usually by allowing manual pointer arithmetic.
Buggy describes code that has errors in general, but memory-unsafe describes a structural property of the language that can make certain bugs possible.

examples.everyday: My friend says C is memory-unsafe, so she avoids it and prefers newer languages.
examples.professional: Most of our legacy codebase is memory-unsafe C, and that is where nearly all of our security findings come from.
examples.analytical: A memory-unsafe language permits pointer arithmetic that can violate the bounds of an allocated object, so correctness depends heavily on programmer discipline.

nuance.analogy: A memory-unsafe language is like a kitchen with no cabinet doors: everything is accessible, which is convenient until someone reaches for the wrong thing.
nuance.etymology: Compound of memory (from Latin memoria) and unsafe (un- from Old English, plus safe from Latin salvus).
common_mistakes: Writing 'memory unsafe' before a noun without the hyphen.
Stressing the prefix un- as if it were the main stress, instead of stressing SAFE.

senses.definition: Quality of being mercurial; mercuriality.

core.definition: The quality of being changeable, quick-tempered or unpredictable in mood or behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'KYOO', and say 'ree-uhl' clearly with a light final '-ness'. Avoid stressing the first syllable, which is the common error borrowed from 'mercury'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes changeability that can seem lively or frustrating depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use mercurialness; they say 'mercurial' as an adjective, as in 'a mercurial boss'. The noun is correct but formal, and mercuriality is an alternative. In everyday talk, 'moodiness' or 'unpredictability' is simpler.

distinctions.note: Moodiness describes a sulky or gloomy temper, while mercurialness describes rapid shifts between many moods, often lively and quick.
Inconsistency is a neutral failure to stay steady, while mercurialness is more vivid and suggests quick, dramatic shifts of temper or taste.

examples.professional: The mercurialness of the client's priorities meant the requirements changed every week, so we froze the scope.
examples.analytical: The mercurialness of human temperament resists the neat typologies that ancient humoral theory promised to supply.

nuance.analogy: Like a weathervane in a storm: the direction changes so fast that no one can say where it will point next.
nuance.etymology: From mercurial plus -ness; mercurial comes from Latin Mercurius, the god of swift movement, after whom the metal and the planet were named.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in MUR-kyuh-ree; the stress falls on the second syllable.
Confusing it with the metal mercury; this noun names a temper, not an element.

senses.definition: One who brings messages.
The secretary bird.
senses.example: On the African savanna, the messenger stalked snakes through the tall grass while we watched through binoculars.

senses.definition: The supporting member of an aerial cable (electric power or telephone or data).
senses.example: The utility crew replaced the rusted messenger wire that held the fiber line above Elm Street.

senses.definition: A person appointed to perform certain ministerial duties under bankrupt and insolvent laws, such as to take charge of the estate of the bankrupt or insolvent.
senses.example: The court appointed a messenger to inventory the debtor's assets and manage the estate until the hearing.

senses.definition: An instant messenger program.
senses.example: Our data team coordinates through instant messenger, so most quick questions never reach email.

senses.definition: A forerunner or harbinger.
senses.example: a messenger of doom

senses.definition: A light scudding cloud preceding a storm.
senses.example: Long before the thunder, a thin messenger cloud raced across the sky above the prairie.

senses.definition: A piece of paper, etc. blown up a string to a kite.
senses.example: We tied a paper messenger to the string, and it slid up the kite line toward the sky.

senses.definition: A weight dropped down a line to close a Nansen bottle.
senses.example: The oceanographer dropped a brass messenger down the line to close the Nansen bottle at depth.

senses.definition: A pin which travels across the pin deck to knock over another pin, usually for a strike.
senses.example: The bowling alley's automatic pinsetter sent a messenger across the deck to finish the rack.

senses.definition: A light line with which a heavier line may be hauled e.g. from the deck of a ship to the pier.
senses.example: Before hauling the heavy mooring cable, the deckhand pulled the messenger line ashore to the pier.

senses.definition: To send something by messenger.
senses.example: I'll messenger over the signed documents.

core.definition: A person or thing that carries a message from one person or place to another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MES. The second syllable is a reduced uh, so the word has only two strong sounds. Many learners add an extra vowel between the s and n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use messenger for a person who delivers a message, such as a courier, and in phrases like shoot the messenger. Today it also appears in instant messaging apps. In casual talk, people more often say courier or delivery person for business deliveries.

distinctions.note: A courier is a paid professional for deliveries, while a messenger is anyone who carries a message, sometimes informally.
An envoy is an official representative sent with diplomatic authority, while a messenger simply carries information.

examples.everyday: Don't shoot the messenger, but the store says the package will be late.
examples.professional: We used a bike messenger to deliver the signed contracts across downtown.
examples.analytical: The prophet presents himself as a messenger whose authority depends entirely on the one who sent him.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay runner passing a baton, a messenger carries something from one hand to the next without changing it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English messager, from Old French message.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, as in mess-en-ger
Confusing messenger with message, which is the thing carried
nuance.biblical_note: In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word mal'ak means messenger, and it is also translated angel. In the New Testament, the Greek word angelos has the same range of meaning. Malachi 3:1 speaks of God sending a messenger to prepare the way. Matthew 11:10 applies that prophecy to John the Baptist, and Luke 7:24-27 describes messengers sent by John to Jesus.

messenger.etymology: From Middle English *messengere*, *messingere*, *messangere*, from Old French *messanger*, a variant of Old French *messagier*, equivalent to *message* + *-er*.

senses.definition: A bishop empowered to oversee other bishops; an archbishop.
senses.example: The metropolitan of the region ordained three new priests during Easter week.

senses.definition: The inhabitant of a metropolis.
senses.example: Most metropolitans rarely think about where their electricity comes from.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the see or province of a metropolitan.
senses.example: The metropolitan province includes eight dioceses under the archbishop's authority.

senses.definition: Of, or pertaining to, a metropolis or other large urban settlement.
senses.example: Metropolitan housing shortages have pushed many young families toward the suburbs.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the parent state of a colony or territory, or the home country, e.g. metropolitan France.
senses.example: The colonial governor was recalled to metropolitan France after the uprising.

core.definition: In many Christian churches, a bishop who presides over a province of bishops, ranking above ordinary bishops; an archbishop.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, 'PAH', with the cot-caught vowel 'ah'. The first syllable has secondary stress, and the ending is weak 'ih-tun'. Don't stress 'MET'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and formal; it indicates rank and authority in church governance.
nuance.usage_note: In church talk, it is a title mainly in Orthodox and some Catholic or Anglican contexts, as in 'Metropolitan Philip'. The adjective for a big city (the 'metropolitan area') is far more common in everyday American English.

distinctions.note: In the Roman Catholic Church a metropolitan is an archbishop who heads a province, while in Orthodoxy 'metropolitan' is often a rank equal to or higher than archbishop.
A patriarch ranks above a metropolitan and leads an autocephalous or major church.
A bishop heads one diocese and is under the metropolitan in a province.

examples.everyday: The metropolitan visited our parish this weekend and served the Liturgy.
examples.professional: The metropolitan has authority over all the bishops in the province.
examples.analytical: The metropolitan's office developed to coordinate bishops within a civil province, linking church order to imperial administration.

nuance.analogy: A metropolitan is like a bishop of bishops for a region.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin metropolitanus, from Greek mētropolis 'mother city', from mētēr 'mother' + polis 'city'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'MET-ro-pol-i-tan'.
Using 'metropolitan' for a city resident; Americans say 'city dweller' or 'urbanite'.

traditions.view: A metropolitan is a bishop heading a church province or a major see; in some churches the title is an honor for bishops, and the metropolitan presides over a synod.
A metropolitan is the archbishop who heads an ecclesiastical province and has limited oversight over the suffragan bishops under him.

Most Protestant churches have no office of metropolitan; some Anglican provinces have a metropolitan or primate, and Lutheran churches in some countries have archbishops, but many Protestants reject a hierarchy of bishops altogether.

metropolitan.etymology: From Late Latin *mētropolītānus*, from *mētropolis* [itself from Ancient Greek *μητρόπολις*] *-ītānus* [ultimately from *grc:-ίτης* + *-ānus*].

senses.definition: Marked by mettle or bravery; courageous.
senses.example: The mettlesome rookie volunteered to lead the rescue team into the burning building.

core.definition: Full of spirit and courage, eager to face challenges and show determination.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. 'Mettle' sounds exactly like 'metal,' and the final '-some' is reduced to 'sum,' with no strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises spirit, courage, and eagerness, though it can sound slightly old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in writing or in describing animals, especially horses. In casual speech you would more likely say 'spirited' or 'feisty.' It is sometimes used of people in sports or leadership to praise energetic determination.

distinctions.note: 'Spirited' is a general and common word for lively or energetic, while 'mettlesome' adds the idea of courage under test.
'Feisty' is informal and often describes small people or animals who are aggressive or quarrelsome; 'mettlesome' is more formal and admiring.

examples.everyday: The new puppy is mettlesome and wants to chase every squirrel in the yard.
examples.professional: We need a mettlesome team lead who will push back on unrealistic deadlines and defend the engineers.
examples.analytical: Shakespeare's Hotspur is so mettlesome that his courage borders on recklessness, which makes his fall more tragic.

nuance.analogy: A mettlesome person is like a strong steel blade: it bends under pressure but does not break, and it springs back ready for the next challenge.
nuance.etymology: Mettle is an originally identical form of metal, whose figurative sense of temperament or spirit developed from the idea of a metal's temper; -some means full of.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'mettlesome' with 'metal' in speech, since both are pronounced the same, but only 'metal' is the material.
Using 'mettlesome' for a person who is aggressive or rude, when it actually means spirited and courageous.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of a mire; swampy, boggy.
senses.example: After the flood, our boots sank into the miry ground at the edge of the cornfield.

core.definition: Covered with or full of deep, wet, sticky mud; swampy or boggy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the r is pronounced. The second syllable is a light 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes ground that is unpleasant and hard to move through.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'miry' mainly in literature, poetry, and Bible reading, and rarely in speech. In everyday talk they say 'muddy' or 'swampy'. The word can sound a bit old-fashioned if used casually.

distinctions.note: 'Muddy' is the everyday word, while 'miry' is more literary and suggests deeper, stickier ground.
'Boggy' describes wet, spongy ground, while 'miry' focuses on thick, clinging mud.

examples.everyday: We walked along the miry path after the rain, and my boots were caked in mud.
examples.professional: The site inspection report noted miry ground near the drainage pipes, which will slow the crew.
examples.analytical: The psalmist's image of a miry pit becomes a figure for distress and deliverance in the Psalter.

nuance.analogy: Like a boot pulled slowly out of thick clay, something miry holds on to you as you move.
nuance.etymology: From 'mire' with the adjective ending '-y'.
common_mistakes: Using 'miry' in everyday speech where 'muddy' is more natural.
Pronouncing it as 'MY-ur-ee' with an extra syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, 'miry' describes the pit or bog from which God rescues the one in distress. Psalm 40:2 describes God drawing the psalmist up from a miry bog. Psalm 69:2 speaks of sinking in deep mire without footing. Jeremiah 38:6 describes Jeremiah being lowered into a cistern where there is mire.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being mischievous; the tendency to make mischief.
senses.example: The twins' mischievousness showed in the whoopee cushion hidden under Grandma's chair.

core.definition: The quality of being playful and inclined to tease or cause small, harmless trouble.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the word has four syllables with the final '-ness' pronounced as a reduced 'nus'. Avoid adding an extra syllable in the middle, as in 'mis-chee-VUS-ness'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly positive to neutral; it describes a playful personality, though it can suggest a lack of seriousness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually prefer a phrase such as 'a mischievous streak' or 'a mischievous look' in everyday speech. The noun 'mischievousness' appears more often in writing, reviews and descriptions of character. It is safe to use when describing someone's temperament, but you may sound stiff in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Mischief is the act or the trouble itself, while mischievousness is the underlying quality or tendency.
Malice is an intention to harm others, which is much more serious than the playful quality described by mischievousness.

examples.everyday: There's a glint of mischievousness in her eyes whenever she's planning a surprise party.
examples.professional: His mischievousness made him a memorable speaker, though a few of his jokes landed badly with the audience.
examples.analytical: The ironic mischievousness of the text disarms the reader, so that its moral claims seem both sincere and unreliable.

nuance.analogy: Like a sparkle in the eye: small, bright and hard to ignore, but not dangerous.
nuance.etymology: From 'mischievous', from Anglo-French 'meschevous', plus the noun ending '-ness'.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable and saying 'mis-chee-VUS-ness'; the word is simpler than it looks.
Using 'mischievousness' in casual speech where 'mischievous streak' sounds more natural to Americans.

senses.definition: To manipulate something roughly, causing physical damage.
senses.example: If you mishandle a fragile package, the contents may break.

senses.definition: To deal with a situation incorrectly or ineffectively; to make a mistake in handling a situation.
senses.example: The prime minister was accused of mishandling the diplomatic crisis.

senses.definition: Rough manipulation which causes physical damage.
senses.example: The moving crew mishandled the antique dresser, cracking two legs on the stairs.

senses.definition: Ineffective or incorrect deal.
senses.example: The city's mishandle of the flood response left thousands of families waiting for weeks.

senses.definition: Improper, wrong, or bad usage or treatment; abuse.
senses.example: Her lawyer argued that the hospital's mishandle of patient records violated privacy law.

core.definition: To deal with something or someone badly or incorrectly, causing a poor result, or to handle something roughly and damage it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, HAN. The final -dle is a syllabic 'dul' with no extra vowel between the d and the l, so say it as one quick syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies a mistake or carelessness that caused a bad result, so it sounds like criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mishandle' often in news, workplace and everyday complaints, as in 'the company mishandled the complaint'. It can refer to physical rough treatment, as in 'don't mishandle the package'. The noun 'mishandling' is common in formal reports and reviews.

distinctions.note: Mismanage focuses on poor control of a whole operation or budget, while mishandle often refers to a specific situation or item.
Botch is informal and suggests a clumsy, sloppy failure, while mishandle is more neutral and can describe a serious error.

examples.everyday: The airline really mishandled my luggage, and it took three days to get my bag back.
examples.professional: We mishandled the handoff between the data team and the product team, so the dashboard shipped with the wrong metric.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the government mishandled the early response, which made the eventual reform more costly and less trusted.

nuance.analogy: Like a fragile vase carried with a careless grip, a mishandled situation can break something valuable even when the intention was good.
nuance.etymology: From mis- (wrongly) plus 'handle', from Old English handlian, to touch or manage.
common_mistakes: Using 'mishandling' as a verb; the verb is 'mishandle' and the noun is 'mishandling'.
Stressing the first syllable as MIS-han-dul; the stress belongs on the second syllable.

senses.definition: To lead astray, in a false direction.
senses.example: The GPS voice kept misleading us down a gravel road that dead-ended at a farm.

senses.definition: To deceive by telling lies or otherwise giving a false impression.
senses.example: The company's ads were designed to mislead customers about the true cost of the loan.

senses.definition: To deceptively trick into something wrong.
senses.example: The preacher elaborated Satan's ways to mislead us into sin

senses.definition: To accidentally or intentionally confuse.
senses.example: I'm sorry, the instructions were confusing and I think I misled you about the deadline.

senses.definition: A wrong or bad lead; a leading in the wrong direction.
senses.example: The anonymous tip was a mislead that sent detectives chasing the wrong suspect.

senses.definition: That which is deceptive or untruthful (e.g. a falsehood, deception, untruth, or ruse).
senses.example: Everything the senator said in that interview was a mislead designed to hide the scandal.

core.definition: To cause someone to believe something false or to act wrongly, by giving wrong information or a false impression.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, LEED, which rhymes with 'need'. The past tense is 'misled', pronounced 'mis-LED', so do not say 'mis-leaded'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that someone was led into error, often by an ad, a statement, or a leader, and it can suggest intent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use this verb about advertising, politicians, or wrong instructions: 'The sign misled me.' It is common in news and in complaints to companies. In casual talk, people say 'I was misled' to explain that they were given bad information. For outright lies, Americans may use 'lie to' or 'deceive' instead.

distinctions.note: Deceive means to intentionally make someone believe something untrue; mislead can describe either intention or honest error.
Lie means to say something you know is false; mislead can be done through facts that are technically true but arranged to confuse.

examples.everyday: Do not let the online photos mislead you; the hotel is much smaller than it looks.
examples.professional: The slide was designed to mislead the reader into thinking the numbers had improved, so please fix the chart.
examples.analytical: A statement may mislead without being false, since selective emphasis can create an impression the facts do not fully support.

nuance.analogy: To mislead someone is like giving a traveler a map with a river drawn in the wrong place: he walks confidently in the wrong direction.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'misleden', from 'mis-' meaning wrongly plus 'lead', from Old English 'lædan'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the past tense 'misled' as 'mis-LEE-did'; the past tense rhymes with 'red'.
Using 'mislead' for simple factual errors; for an honest mistake, 'misinform' or 'misinterpret' may fit better.

mislead.etymology: From Middle English *mysleden*, from Old English *mislǣdan* (“to mislead”), from Proto-Germanic **missalaidijaną* (“to mislead”).

senses.definition: An incorrect specification.
senses.example: The regression results were biased by a misspecification of the income variable.

core.definition: An error in defining a statistical or machine learning model, such as using the wrong functional form or leaving out relevant variables, so it does not match reality.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KAY, with weaker stress on the first mis-. Say the double s as one held s sound, not two sounds with a vowel between them.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a modeling error rather than a moral failing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in statistics, econometrics and machine learning to describe a model whose assumptions or structure are wrong. In meetings, people more often say 'the model is misspecified' than use the noun. It is a precise technical term, so outside technical contexts it may sound jargon-heavy.

distinctions.note: Overfitting means a model learns noise in the training data, while misspecification means its basic structure is wrong even with plenty of data.
Underfitting means a model is too simple to capture real patterns, and misspecification can cause it but refers to any wrong assumption about form.
Bias is a general systematic error in estimates, while misspecification is one specific cause of bias.

examples.everyday: My roommate said my running model was off because I left hills out of it, which is a kind of misspecification.
examples.professional: Before we trust these regression results, we should check for misspecification in the functional form and missing variables.
examples.analytical: A regression that omits a relevant confounder suffers from misspecification, so its coefficients answer a different question than the one we intended.

nuance.analogy: Misspecification is like measuring a room with a bent ruler: you get numbers, but they describe the wrong shape.
nuance.etymology: From English mis- (wrongly) and specification, from Medieval Latin specificatio, from specificare, 'to make specific'.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on the first syllable; the strongest stress is on -CAY-.
Using the word for any error; it names a wrong model setup or assumption, not a general mistake.

senses.definition: In a misty manner.

core.definition: In a misty or hazy way, with a soft blurred look or with tearful, dreamy eyes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a short, unstressed 'ih' vowel. The final -ly is pronounced as a clear 'lee,' not 'lie.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive: it creates a soft, poetic image, though it can suggest sadness or nostalgia depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mistily' mainly in descriptive or literary writing, such as novels, poems, travel writing, and essays about memory. In everyday speech people more often say 'hazily' for weather or 'teary-eyed' for emotion. You will rarely hear it in casual conversation, but you will meet it in books and well-written prose.

distinctions.note: 'Foggily' describes fog or confused thinking, while 'mistily' usually describes a softer, lighter haze or a dreamy or tearful look.
'Dimly' stresses low light or faint awareness, while 'mistily' emphasizes a blurred, veiled appearance.

examples.everyday: The hills looked mistily blue from the porch this morning.
examples.professional: The photographs were taken early, so the skyline appears mistily soft in every frame.
examples.analytical: The narrator recalls her childhood mistily, so the reader cannot tell which memories are real and which have been shaped by longing.

nuance.analogy: Like a window fogged by warm breath, where the view is still there but softened.
nuance.etymology: From 'misty' (from Old English 'mist,' meaning fog or vapor) plus the suffix '-ly.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'mistily' with 'mystically,' which means in a spiritual or mysterious way.
Using 'mistily' in casual speech, where 'hazily' or 'teary-eyed' would sound more natural.

senses.definition: To understand incorrectly, while believing one has understood correctly.

core.definition: To understand something or someone incorrectly, thinking you have understood correctly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'stand,' the last syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, so 'un' sounds like 'uhn' and 'der' sounds like a short r-colored schwa. Keep the 'd' clear and do not add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a plain description of a mistake, though it can sound annoyed when repeated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'misunderstand' constantly in everyday speech, often to correct someone politely, as in 'I think you misunderstood me.' The phrase 'Don't misunderstand me' is a common softener before criticism. A natural reply is 'Oh, sorry, I got that wrong,' or 'Let me explain.'

distinctions.note: 'Mishear' means hearing words incorrectly, while 'misunderstand' means getting the meaning wrong, even if you heard the words correctly.
'Misinterpret' is more formal and is used for texts, data, evidence, or actions, while 'misunderstand' is common in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I misunderstood you, I thought you wanted to meet at noon.
examples.professional: I think the client misunderstood the scope, so let's confirm the deliverables in writing.
examples.analytical: Many critics misunderstand the author's irony, taking a satire of nationalism as a straightforward patriotic statement.

nuance.analogy: Like reading a map upside down: you can see the lines clearly and still reach the wrong place.
nuance.etymology: From 'mis-' (wrongly) plus 'understand,' from Old English 'understandan.'
common_mistakes: Writing 'misunderstand about' instead of 'misunderstand' with a direct object, such as 'misunderstand the instructions.'
Confusing it with 'mishear,' which describes hearing words wrongly rather than misreading meaning.

senses.definition: During, or by means of, mitosis.
senses.example: The cells divided mitotically, so each daughter cell received an identical copy of the chromosomes.

core.definition: In a way that happens by mitosis, the process in which a cell divides into two genetically identical cells.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TAH, and let the final -ly become a light ee sound. Do not add an extra vowel before the -cal-style ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term used to describe a process.
nuance.usage_note: Found in research papers and lab reports, often to describe how cells grow or multiply. Most speakers would say by mitosis or through mitosis in casual speech. The adverb is used mostly with verbs such as divide, proliferate or replicate.

distinctions.note: By mitosis is the more common phrase in everyday and mixed-audience writing, while mitotically is more compact and used in technical reports.

examples.everyday: The doctor said the cells in that growth are dividing mitotically, which is why it is getting bigger.
examples.professional: The tumor cells were proliferating mitotically, and the pathologist confirmed it with a special stain.
examples.analytical: Cells that divide mitotically preserve the parent genome, whereas meiotically produced cells reshuffle it.

nuance.analogy: Dividing mitotically is like a cell making an exact copy of its own instructions for the next cell.
nuance.etymology: From mitotic plus the adverb suffix -ally, from Greek mitos (thread).
common_mistakes: Using the adjective mitotic where the adverb mitotically is needed, as in 'the cells divide mitotic'.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: To stir together.
senses.example: Mix the eggs and milk with the flour until the consistency is smooth.

senses.definition: To combine (items from two or more sources normally kept separate).
senses.example: to mix business with pleasure

senses.definition: To form by mingling; to produce by the stirring together of ingredients; to concoct from different parts.
senses.example: Yellow and blue paint mix to make green.

senses.definition: To blend by the use of a mixer (machine).
senses.example: Mix the egg whites until they are stiff.

senses.definition: To unite with in company; to join; to associate.
To combine (several tracks).
senses.example: I'll mix the rhythm tracks down to a single track.

senses.definition: To produce a finished version of (a recording).
senses.example: I'm almost done mixing this song.

senses.definition: The result of mixing two or more substances; a mixture.
senses.example: Now add the raisins to the mix.

senses.definition: The result of combining items normally kept separate.
senses.example: My recipe file was now a mix of meat and dairy.

senses.definition: A preparation, usually in the form of a powder, into which other ingredients can be mixed to prepare a specified foodstuff.
senses.example: Cake mix. Pancake mix. Hot chocolate mix.

senses.definition: A substance used to dilute or adulterate an illicit drug.
The result of mixing several tracks.
senses.example: The rhythm mix sounds muddy.

senses.definition: The finished version of a recording.
senses.example: I've almost finished the mix for this song.

core.definition: To combine two or more things, such as ingredients or data, so that they become one mass or group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable, and keep the short i vowel. Do not add an extra vowel between the m and the k or between the x sound and the s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an ordinary action and can be used in cooking, mixing music or combining information.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mix constantly in cooking, business and everyday talk. Mix can be followed by with or into, depending on the object. Many learners overuse mix up for everything, but mix up often means confuse or mistake.

distinctions.note: Stir means moving something in circles with a spoon, while mix is broader and can mean combining with any tool or by hand.
Blend often means combining smooth or liquid items into a uniform texture, while mix is more general.

examples.everyday: Can you mix the batter while I finish preheating the oven?
examples.professional: I'll mix the two datasets on the customer ID before we train the model.
examples.analytical: Such arguments mix empirical claims with moral ones, which makes it hard to see what the evidence actually shows.

nuance.analogy: Mixing is like shuffling two decks of cards until you cannot tell which card came from which deck.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English mixen, from Old English miscian, related to mengan, to mix.
common_mistakes: Saying mix up when you mean only mix, which may change the meaning to confuse.
Using mix as a noun without a determiner in countable contexts, such as 'a mix of ingredients' instead of 'mix of ingredients'.

mix.etymology: From Middle English *mixen* (attested in past tense as *mixed*, *myxyd*), from Old English **mixian*, *miscian*, from **miskijan*, from **miskijan* (“to mix”), from Proto-Indo-European, from **meyǵ-*, **meyḱ-* (“to mix”).

senses.definition: Through the use of mnemonics.
senses.example: The students learned the planets' order mnemonically, using a silly sentence.

senses.definition: As a mnemonic.
senses.example: The rhyme works mnemonically, so the kids remember the spelling rule.

core.definition: In a way that uses a memory aid, such as a rhyme, acronym, or pattern, to help remember something.

pronunciation.tip: The initial m is silent, so start with a soft 'nuh' sound and stress the second syllable, 'MAH'. The ending '-ly' is a light 'lee', not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a method of learning and sounds academic in ordinary talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mnemonically mainly in teaching, science, medicine, and music, where a memory device is being explained. In casual speech, people say 'as a memory trick' or 'to remember it' instead. The adverb is less common than the noun mnemonic, so use it when describing how something is learned or stored.

distinctions.note: By rote means by repetition alone, without understanding, while mnemonically means with the help of a memory aid.
Memorably describes something that is easy to remember, not the technique used to remember it.

examples.everyday: My son learned the order of the planets mnemonically, using a silly sentence his teacher made up.
examples.professional: We organize the API parameters mnemonically, grouping related fields under short prefixes so developers can recall them.
examples.analytical: Ancient orators organized long speeches mnemonically, placing each argument in a familiar room of the mind.

nuance.analogy: Like tying a string on your finger, a mnemonic attaches meaning to something that is easy to recall.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mnēmonikos 'of memory', from mnēmōn 'mindful'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a noun, as in 'a good mnemonically'; the noun is mnemonic.
Pronouncing the initial m, as in 'm-nuh-MAH-nik'; the m is silent.

senses.definition: Someone able to perform feats of memory, especially by using mnemonic techniques.
senses.example: The mnemonist could recite a shuffled deck of cards after one brief glance.

core.definition: A person with exceptional memory who uses memory techniques to recall large amounts of information, such as long lists or numbers.

pronunciation.tip: The m is silent, so begin with 'n'. Stress the second syllable, 'MAH', and keep the final '-ist' short, rhyming with 'list'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and admiring, suggesting trained skill; it is rarely used as an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mnemonist mostly in psychology, education, and discussions of memory competitions, where people are described by their technique. In everyday speech, people more often say 'memory champion' or 'someone with a great memory'. Calling someone a mnemonist usually implies training in memory systems, not just a natural gift.

distinctions.note: Memory champion stresses competition and results, while mnemonist stresses the technique behind the memory.
Photographic memory is a popular term with little scientific support; mnemonist refers to trained, technique-based memory.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a mnemonist who can recite a whole deck of cards in order, which always impresses the kids.
examples.professional: We brought in a mnemonist to demonstrate the training method, and her recall results helped us design the course.
examples.analytical: The mnemonist's achievements suggest that recall depends on structured encoding more than on raw storage capacity.

nuance.analogy: A mnemonist is like a librarian who files every book by a clever system, so any title can be found quickly.
nuance.etymology: From mnemonic plus the suffix -ist, 'one who practices or specializes in'.
common_mistakes: Confusing mnemonist, the person, with mnemonic, the memory aid itself.
Pronouncing the silent m, as in 'm-nih-MAH-nist'.

senses.definition: To become or cause to become modal.
senses.example: Linguists note that the auxiliary verb can modalize a claim about possibility.

core.definition: To make something modal, or to express a claim with modal words such as might, must, or necessarily.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MOH, and the middle syllable is a weak schwa. The ending -ize is pronounced /aɪz/, rhyming with 'lies', not with 'size'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Modalize is used mainly in logic, linguistics and philosophy, where it describes turning a plain statement into a qualified one. Americans use it in academic talk and writing, but rarely in everyday conversation. In everyday speech, people say they are hedging or softening a claim.

distinctions.note: Hedge is an everyday word for softening a statement, while modalize is a technical term for expressing it with modal operators such as necessarily or possibly.

examples.professional: In the forecast memo, we should modalize the revenue estimate so readers see a range rather than a promise.
examples.analytical: To modalize the categorical claim that all swans are white is to restate it as necessarily all swans are white, which changes its logical status.

nuance.analogy: Modalizing a claim is like adding a weather forecast to a plan: it says what is likely, not what is certain.
nuance.etymology: From modal, from Medieval Latin modalis and Latin modus 'measure, manner', plus the suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Using it in everyday conversation, where hedge or soften sounds more natural
Confusing it with modulate, which means to vary or adjust a signal or a voice

senses.definition: To make modular.

core.definition: To divide a system, design, or program into separate, interchangeable parts or modules that can be developed and tested independently.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllables are reduced to 'juh-luh'. Learners often insert an extra vowel or stress the final -ize, which should be a light 'eyes' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a design approach and carries a generally positive sense of making systems easier to manage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use modularize mainly in software engineering, hardware design, and systems architecture. In everyday talk, people might say break into pieces or split up. In meetings, modularize is common when discussing how to restructure code or a product.

distinctions.note: Refactor means to restructure code without changing its behavior; modularize specifically means to organize the code into separate modules.
Decompose means to break down a problem or system into parts; modularize adds the goal of making those parts interchangeable and independent.
Componentize is similar but common in web and UI development, while modularize is the broader software and systems term.

examples.everyday: My brother works on home automation, and he is trying to modularize his smart-home setup so each device can be replaced separately.
examples.professional: Let's modularize the data pipeline so the ingestion step can be tested without running the whole model.
examples.analytical: A theory of knowledge that modularizes cognition into independent faculties faces difficult questions about how the modules communicate.

nuance.analogy: To modularize a system is like building with LEGO bricks instead of carving one solid block: each brick can be swapped or reused without breaking the whole.
nuance.etymology: From modular, from module, from Latin modulus meaning 'small measure', plus the verb suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Using modularize without an object, which sounds unclear; say modularize the code or the system.
Confusing modularize with modulate, which means to vary or adjust a tone or signal.

senses.definition: Modification or regulation of something to achieve an appropriate measure or proportion; an instance of this.
senses.example: Garamond has much modulation, while Helvetica has very little.

senses.definition: Variation (especially softening or toning down) of brightness, form, etc. an instance of this.
senses.example: The painter's careful modulation of light made the room feel warm and calm.

senses.definition: Variation of the intensity, pitch, and tone of the sound of a musical instrument or voice; inflection; an instance of this.
senses.example: Her voice showed subtle modulation as she moved from pleading to firm reassurance.

senses.definition: Changing of the key in a piece of music; also, the effect achieved by this as an element of harmony; an instance of this.
senses.example: The song's modulation to E major gives the final chorus its uplifting lift.

senses.definition: The quality of a typeface of having contrasting, thick and thin parts of the strokes; stroke-width variation.
senses.example: Garamond has much modulation, while Helvetica has very little.

senses.definition: Changing of a thing from one form to another; an instance of this.
senses.example: The chemist studied the modulation of energy from heat into electrical current.

senses.definition: Harmonious use of language in poetry or prose.
senses.example: The poem's modulation of sound, from harsh consonants to soft vowels, delighted my professor.

senses.definition: Any of the musical notes in ecclesiastical modes of music on which a melodic phrase had to begin and end.
senses.example: In Gregorian chant, each melodic phrase had to begin and end on a proper modulation.

senses.definition: Arrangement or composition, or performance, of music in a certain key or mode; also a series of musical notes, chord, or tune analyzed according to a key or mode.
senses.example: The hymn's modulation through the Dorian mode gave the old melody a haunting quality.

senses.definition: Making music or singing; a melody, a tune; also, a musical note.
senses.example: Let every soul join in the modulation of praise that rises from this humble congregation.

senses.definition: Variation in the activity or form of a cell in response to changes in the environment; an instance of this.
senses.example: Stress hormones trigger a rapid modulation of gene expression in cells exposed to heat.

senses.definition: Chiefly preceded by a descriptive word: modification of an electromagnetic wave or other oscillating carrier wave to apply a signal to it; an instance of this; also, the extent to which such a wave is modified; and the modified wave or signal.
senses.example: Engineers compared amplitude modulation and frequency modulation for the new radio link.

senses.definition: (rare) Modification of the parts of a classical Greek or Roman building to achieve appropriate proportions by measuring in modules (“standard units of measure, usually the diameter or radius of a column at the base of a shaft”).
senses.example: The architect adjusted the column modulation so the temple's proportions looked balanced from below.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The controlled change or adjustment of a signal's property, such as amplitude, frequency, or pitch, to carry information or achieve an effect.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the -lay syllable, and the ending -ation is pronounced shun, not shuh-nay. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce every vowel fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is value-free and describes a deliberate, controlled change, so it carries no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers, data scientists and audio specialists use modulation constantly, for example in radio, signal processing and machine learning. In everyday speech Americans might say the voice has good modulation, meaning variation in pitch and tone, but the word is more typical in technical or musical contexts. In music, the same word refers to a change of key, which is a separate sense.

distinctions.note: Adjustment is any small change made to fit a purpose, while modulation is a systematic variation of a carrier signal or sound property.
Modification is a general change to something's form or design, whereas modulation specifically means regulated variation of a wave or signal.
Inflection is the rise and fall of a speaker's voice, a common everyday word, while modulation is the broader, more technical term for controlled variation in a sound or signal.

examples.everyday: The radio sounds clearer on FM because it uses frequency modulation.
examples.professional: We switched the link to quadrature amplitude modulation, which doubled throughput without needing more bandwidth.
examples.analytical: Modulation imposes information onto a carrier wave so it can travel across a medium, and the receiver must reverse that process precisely to recover the message.

nuance.analogy: Like a dimmer switch that changes a light's brightness in a controlled way so that it can carry a message.
nuance.etymology: From Latin modulatio, from modulari 'to measure or regulate', related to modus 'measure'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in MOD-yoo-lay-shun.
Using modulation to mean any change, when it refers to a regulated, systematic variation.
Confusing modulation in music, meaning a change of key, with its technical signal sense.

modulation.etymology: An example of modulation in music from the tonic to the dominant.

senses.definition: A valid form of argument in which the antecedent of a conditional proposition is affirmed, thereby entailing the affirmation of the consequent. Modus ponens has the form.
senses.example: 1. If P, then Q.

core.definition: A valid argument form: if P implies Q, and P is true, then Q must be true. Latin for the way of affirming.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first word, MOH, and on the second word, POH. The o in modus is a long oh, and the final s in ponens is a clear z sound, so it sounds like POH-nenz.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; used in logic, philosophy and mathematics classes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use modus ponens mainly in philosophy, logic, computer science, and law courses. Speakers usually add the Latin term to show precision. Often it is shortened to MP in written proofs. In everyday life it is rare, so a casual conversation partner may not recognize it without a short explanation.

distinctions.note: Modus ponens affirms the antecedent to conclude the consequent, while modus tollens denies the consequent to conclude that the antecedent is false.
Affirming the consequent is a fallacy that reasons from Q and P implies Q to P, which is invalid, while modus ponens is valid.
Hypothetical syllogism chains two conditionals together, while modus ponens applies one conditional to a true antecedent.

examples.everyday: If it rains, the game is canceled, and it's raining, so the game is canceled; that's basically modus ponens.
examples.professional: In the verification tool, the rule engine applies modus ponens whenever a premise matches an implication.
examples.analytical: By modus ponens, if the premises hold and the conditional is true, the conclusion follows necessarily.

nuance.analogy: Modus ponens is like a vending machine rule: if you insert the correct coins, then the drink comes out, and once you have inserted them, you know the drink will come out.
nuance.etymology: From Latin modus ponens, meaning the mode that affirms, from modus meaning manner and ponere meaning to place or affirm.
common_mistakes: Confusing modus ponens with the fallacy of affirming the consequent, which reverses the conditional.
Pronouncing modus with a short o, as in MOD-us; in American speech the first vowel is long.

modus-ponens.etymology: From Latin *modus ponendo ponens* (roughly, “mode where affirming affirms”).

senses.definition: A government in which sovereignty is embodied within a single, today usually hereditary head of state (whether as a figurehead or as a powerful ruler).
senses.example: An absolute monarchy is a monarchy where the monarch is legally the ultimate authority in all temporal matters.

senses.definition: The territory ruled over by a monarch; a kingdom.
senses.example: The small monarchy bordered two larger countries and maintained its own currency.

senses.definition: A form of government where sovereignty is embodied by a single ruler in a state and his high aristocracy representing their separate divided lands within the state and their low aristocracy representing their separate divided fiefs.
senses.example: Under the old monarchy, sovereignty rested with one ruler and his feudal lords.

senses.definition: States based on a system of governance headed by a king or a queen.

core.definition: A form of government headed by a single ruler, usually a king or queen who inherits the position, who may have real power or serve as a symbolic figurehead.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a weak, rhotic schwa rather than a full 'ar' sound. Don't add a separate 'ar' vowel after the 'n'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a system of government and carries no judgment by itself; speakers may add positive or negative views depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use monarchy mainly when discussing history, politics, or other countries, such as the British monarchy. The United States has no monarchy, so people often say 'we don't have a king' or 'we got rid of a monarchy in 1776.' Using it in casual talk is fine, but people usually say 'the royal family' when they mean the people themselves.

distinctions.note: Monarchy is the system of government, while a monarch is the single person who rules.
A kingdom is a territory or state ruled by a king, while monarchy refers to the form of government itself.

examples.everyday: My friend is obsessed with the British monarchy, so she watches every royal wedding on TV.
examples.professional: Our research team is comparing how different monarchy systems handle public budget decisions.
examples.analytical: A constitutional monarchy distributes sovereignty between a hereditary head of state and an elected legislature, which makes its legitimacy a question of both tradition and consent.

nuance.analogy: A monarchy is like a family business where power passes from parent to child, even if the children now mostly show up to cut ribbons.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin monarchia, from Greek monarkhia, 'rule by one,' from monos 'alone' and arkhein 'to rule'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'ar' (MAH-nar-kee) instead of a weak 'ur' sound.
Using monarchy to mean a single king rather than the system of government.

monarchy.etymology: From Old French *monarchie*, from Late Latin *monarchia*, from Ancient Greek *μοναρχία*, from *μόνος* (“only”) + *ἀρχή* (“power, authority”).

senses.definition: In a monolithic manner.

core.definition: In a way that is unified and uniform, as if forming one undivided, rigid whole.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'LITH', and the ending '-ically' is pronounced 'ih-klee', with the 'a' of 'ical' reduced to nothing. Many learners say 'lith-ih-cal-ly' with an extra syllable, but Americans compress it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests rigidity, conformity, or a lack of internal variety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use monolithically in political analysis, sociology, and software architecture, usually to say that a group or system acts as one unit with no internal dissent. It is a fairly formal word, so it would sound stiff in casual talk. In conversation people more often say 'all in one block' or 'they all voted the same way'.

distinctions.note: Uniformly means evenly or identically across parts, while monolithically suggests one solid whole that resists division.
Unanimously refers specifically to a vote or decision in which everyone agrees, whereas monolithically describes general behavior or structure.

examples.everyday: The whole family votes monolithically on every school board election, so nobody ever argues about it.
examples.professional: We built the first version monolithically, so every feature change requires redeploying the whole application.
examples.analytical: Scholars have criticized the habit of describing the state as acting monolithically, since it hides real internal conflict.

nuance.analogy: Acting monolithically is like a crowd of people moving as one solid slab, with no one stepping out of line.
nuance.etymology: From monolith, from Greek monolithos 'of one stone', with the suffixes -ic and -ally.
common_mistakes: Using monolithically to mean simply 'completely' or 'entirely', which is not its meaning.
Stressing the wrong syllable as in 'mon-oh-LITH-ik-lee'.
Confusing it with monolingually, which refers to language.

senses.definition: Of a function: that either never decreases or never increases as its independent variable increases.
Of or using the Greek system of diacritics which discards the breathings and employs a single accent to indicate stress. It replaced polytonic system in 1982.
senses.example: Modern Greek textbooks print texts in the monotonic system, which uses a single accent mark.

senses.definition: Uttered in a monotone; monotonous.
senses.example: His monotonic voice put the entire lecture hall to sleep.

core.definition: Of a function: never decreasing or never increasing as its input increases. Used in mathematics and logic.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the third syllable, -TAH-, with a lighter stress on MAH-. The vowel in -tan- is the same as in 'father' in General American, the cot-caught merger sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American mathematics and computer science, monotonic describes functions or sequences that move in one direction only. Americans use it in lectures, papers and code documentation, not in ordinary talk. The sense of 'uttered in a monotone' is not standard in American English, and the Greek diacritics sense belongs to classical scholarship.

distinctions.note: Monotone in mathematics means the same as monotonic, but in everyday English it means an unvarying voice; use monotonic in technical writing.
A monotonic function may have flat stretches, while a strictly monotonic function must always increase or always decrease.

examples.professional: Our loss function is monotonic in the prediction error, so a lower error always gives a lower loss.
examples.analytical: If the utility function is monotonic in wealth, then more wealth never makes the agent worse off, which is the assumption the proof relies on.

nuance.analogy: A staircase that never goes down: it may have flat landings, but it never drops.
nuance.etymology: From Greek monotonos, 'of one tone', via the mathematical sense of 'never changing direction'.
common_mistakes: Using monotonic to describe a boring or unvarying voice in everyday speech; use monotone or monotonous.
Confusing monotonic with monotonous, which is a different word with different meaning and stress.

senses.definition: An act of killing a person unlawfully, especially with predetermination.
senses.example: Throwing that punch was a murder whether you meant for it to happen or not.

senses.definition: Short for felony murder, the act of committing or abetting a crime that results in the killing of a person, regardless of intent, even if the perpetrator did not directly kill the victim.
senses.example: Both the arsonist and her partner were charged with murder, even though they had intended for it to be a victimless crime.

senses.definition: The act of killing any being in an immoral manner; an instance of this.
senses.example: Meat is murder.

senses.definition: Synonym of murderer, a person who has unlawfully killed another.
senses.example: Police finally caught the murder who had terrorized the county for nearly a decade.

senses.definition: Something difficult or terrible to endure.
senses.example: I heard this class is murder.

senses.definition: A flock of crows or sometimes ravens.
senses.example: A murder of crows dotted my backyard.

senses.definition: The crime of killing a person unlawfully, especially with predetermination.
senses.example: The defendant was charged with murder.

senses.definition: (dated) Something remarkable or impressive.
senses.example: That chocolate cake was a murder, honestly the best thing I've eaten all year.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To illegally kill with intent, especially with predetermination.
senses.example: The woman found dead in her kitchen was murdered by her husband.

senses.definition: To kill violently.
senses.example: My uncle’s dog murdered my cat.

senses.definition: To kick someone's ass or chew someone out (used to express one’s anger at somebody).
senses.example: He's torn my best shirt. When I see him, I'll murder him!

senses.definition: To botch or mangle.
senses.example: I murdered the chorus on my first attempt at the new song.

senses.definition: To defeat decisively.
senses.example: Our team is going to murder them.

core.definition: The crime of killing a person unlawfully and on purpose.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a full r-colored vowel. The second syllable is a weak 'er', so don't say 'mur-DER'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. The word signals serious crime and horror, though people also use it loosely for exaggerated frustration.
nuance.usage_note: In legal, news and police language, murder is the standard word for unlawful killing, and Americans distinguish degrees such as first-degree and second-degree. In casual speech people say things like 'I could murder a coffee' to express strong desire, which is humorous and harmless. Avoid joking this way around people who have lost someone to violence.

distinctions.note: Manslaughter is unlawful killing without malice aforethought, as in a sudden fight or by criminal negligence; murder requires intent or malice.
Homicide is the general term for one person killing another, lawful or not; murder is a specific criminal kind of homicide.
Assassination is the murder of a prominent person, usually for political reasons; murder covers the killing of any person.

examples.everyday: Did you hear about the murder on Maple Street? The whole block is talking about it.
examples.professional: The homicide unit reviewed the murder case file and flagged two gaps in the forensic evidence.
examples.analytical: Philosophers ask whether murder differs from killing in kind or only in the intention behind the act.

nuance.analogy: Killing is the category and murder is a specific kind of killing, defined by intent, the way a bruise is one kind of injury among many.
nuance.etymology: From Old English morthor, a Germanic word for killing.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'dur' instead of a weak 'er'.
Calling accidents or self-defense murder; the word implies deliberate, unlawful intent.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, murder is the killing of a human being in violation of God's command. The Hebrew word ratsach means to kill or murder, and the Greek phoneuo means to murder. Genesis 4:8 describes Cain killing his brother Abel, the first murder recorded in Scripture. Exodus 20:13 gives the commandment against killing, which the RSV renders as 'You shall not kill.' Matthew 15:19 lists murders among the evil things that come from the human heart, showing that the sin begins inwardly.

murder.etymology: From Middle English *murder*, *murdre*, *mourdre*, alteration of earlier *murthre* (“murder”) (see *murther*), from Old English *morþor* (“secret slaying, unlawful killing”) and, both from **morþr*, from Proto-Germanic **murþrą* (“death, killing, murder”),…

senses.definition: In a musical manner.
senses.example: The wind chimes tinkled musically in the breeze.

senses.definition: In terms of music.
senses.example: The film looked good, but was musically lacking.

core.definition: In a way that relates to music or shows a good sense of music; in terms of music.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MYOO. The final syllable is a clear lee, and the middle syllables are reduced, so say kuh-lee rather than kal-ee.

nuance.connotation: Positive when praising a performance or a person's talent; neutral when describing a field.
